catalogTitle: ביטול כח עמלק שבזמן הזה; הסבר יסודות האמונה וביטול דיעות האפיקורסים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Amalek's power is to explain everything as chance, and that the war against Amalek in Adar means seeing Hashem's hand in every event and knowing the foundations of emunah that no theory can shake.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the joy of Adar and the war against Amalek, whose essence is mikreh, chance: when all the chiefs of Edom trembled at the splitting of the sea, Amalek was not impressed. He recalls reading in Graetz's history that a freak wind split the sea, and brings the Ruzhiner's answer to a maskil that such a coincidence is an even greater miracle. The Megillah is a chain of such 'coincidences', and it teaches to see Hashem's hand in nature. He then explains why the Jewish emunah cannot be denied: an entire nation heard Hashem speak at Sinai, unlike religions founded on one individual, and he brings the Yismach Moshe on a mass event passed down from father to son. After explaining why one must speak about this today, he shows that evolution and the age-of-the-world theories are shifting speculation, and closes that the war against Amalek is knowing that every event comes from Hashem.

en: Amalek's essence is mikreh: he attributes everything to chance and denies hashgacha pratis.
Explaining the splitting of the sea as a coincidental wind is no more logical than a miracle; such a coincidence would itself be a greater miracle.
The Megillah is a chain of apparent coincidences, and it teaches to see Hashem's hand within nature.
Jewish emunah rests on what an entire nation saw and heard at Sinai, not on the claim of one individual.
An event witnessed by a multitude and passed on from father to son cannot be denied, just as no one denies Alexander the Great.
Evolution and the calculations of the world's age are shifting theories built on extrapolations that cannot be relied on.
The war against Amalek today is to know that every occurrence, in the world and in one's own life, comes from Hashem.

title.en: Adar, Amalek and chance

summary.en: The Rav opens with the joy of Adar and the war against Amalek, whose essence is chance, as Haman called his downfall 'a coincidence'. He asks why Amalek, alone among the chiefs of Edom, was not shaken by the splitting of the sea.

title.en: Graetz's wind and the Ruzhiner's answer

summary.en: The Rav recalls the apikorsus of the Yiddish papers in his youth and how he read in Graetz's history that a freak wind split the sea. He argues this is not more logical than a miracle, and brings the Ruzhiner's answer that such timing would be an even greater miracle.

title.en: The Megillah's chain of coincidences

summary.en: The Rav goes through the Megillah as a series of 'just then' events, from Vashti to Charvonah, and explains that it teaches to see Hashem's hand in nature, which is the destruction of Amalek. Amalek's attack before Matan Torah cooled the acceptance of the Torah until it was accepted anew in the days of Achashverosh.

title.en: An entire nation heard Hashem speak

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Jewish emunah cannot be denied because six hundred thousand men with their families heard Hashem at Sinai, unlike Christianity, founded on one individual. He adds that milah is kept because of the command at Sinai, and that the people believe in Moshe Rabbeinu because they heard Hashem appoint him.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe on a mass event

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe's answer to someone troubled by doubts in emunah: not to philosophize, but to rely on what a whole multitude saw, which cannot be denied, as no one denies Alexander the Great. The Torah was seen by millions, written and handed down from father to son, and even the other religions admit it, only claiming that Hashem changed His mind, which cannot be.

title.en: Why these matters must be spoken of today

summary.en: The Rav says he never spoke of these matters publicly, since it was not the custom, but today everyone comes into contact with these ideas, and the Skverer Rebbe says one must speak to children and bachurim. He mentions a doctor who began explaining evolution to him when he came for medical advice.

title.en: The folly of a world that made itself

summary.en: The Rav compares the claim that the world came about by itself to saying that a wise, beautifully written sefer was splashed onto its pages by a wind blowing over a bottle of ink, or that a computer evolved by itself. He notes that universities teach evolution only as a theory and that the more science learns, the less sense the theories make.

title.en: Scientific theories keep changing

summary.en: The Rav shows how theories change: the sun was held to circle the earth, Copernicus reversed it, and with Einstein's relativity both views are equally valid. He explains that scientists are driven by the wish for new discoveries and fame, and that belief in the Creator would bind them to the mitzvos, so their claims about billions of years are speculation.

title.en: Why their dating cannot be trusted

summary.en: The Rav explains how a thermometer is built on a measured rate of expansion, and how water surprises by expanding again as it freezes, so no rate can be extrapolated back over a billion years. The same holds for the salt in the sea, rock layers and dinosaur bones: other conditions of pressure and temperature may have existed, and their proofs contradict each other.

title.en: The Mabul and the harmony of creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the boiling waters of the Mabul, covering even the highest mountains, could bring about in a short time changes they calculate as taking a billion years, like a potato that softens in minutes when cooked. He then points to the harmony of creation and compares the unseen life in a creature to electricity in a wire, known by its effects.

title.en: The war against Amalek today

summary.en: The Rav returns to Amalek, who called even the splitting of the sea a coincidence, and says today's devices bring Amalek's influence into the home. The war against Amalek is to know that every event is from Hashem, as the Megillah teaches and as the Ramban writes, and he closes with brachos for the coming year and for the geulah.

catalogTitle: The Multiplied קדושה and Cleansing Power of יו”כ when it Coincides with שבת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Yom Kippur which falls on Shabbos carries a compounded kedushah and a cleansing power beyond that of an ordinary Yom Kippur, and calls for a Shabbos kept in true kedushah.

abstract.en: After explaining why he speaks in English, the Rav cites Chazal's reading of 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the ten days of teshuvah, when the Shechinah comes down to us. The Ba'alei Mussar explain it through the Gemara in Yoma about the butcher who ignored Rav standing at his door: the opportunity is a blessing, but a warning to whoever lets it pass. On Yom Kippur the kedushah comes to every Jew, and the Sefer Torah is carried around for everyone to ask its forgiveness. A Yom Kippur on Shabbos is a double Shabbos; the Arvei Nachal's mashal shows Shabbos and Torah as the king's children who plead for Klal Yisrael. The Rav then urges a Shabbos of real kedushah, without newspapers or idle talk. He concludes, citing the Taz, that Shabbos together with Yom Kippur atones even for sins Yom Kippur alone cannot, and that the world's turmoil is a time to hope for Moshiach.

en: Chazal read 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the ten days of teshuvah, when Hashem lowers Himself and makes Himself available to us.
Hashem's availability is a blessing, but whoever ignores it, like the butcher who ignored Rav, is punished all the more.
When Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos, each strengthens the other and the kedushah of the day is compounded.
Keeping the prohibitions of Shabbos is not enough; Shabbos must be made holy with Torah, tefillah and song, not newspapers or idle talk.
Shabbos together with Yom Kippur atones even for sins that Yom Kippur alone leaves a mark on.

title.en: Seek Hashem when He is found

summary.en: The Rav explains why he speaks in English, then brings Chazal's reading of 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatz'o' as the time the Shechinah descends to us. The Ba'alei Mussar explain it with the Gemara in Yoma about Rav, who went to a butcher who had not asked his forgiveness, and the butcher who ignored him and died.

title.en: An opportunity and a warning

summary.en: The Rav draws the lesson: in the ten days the Shechinah comes down to inspire teshuvah, but woe to one who ignores it. On Yom Kippur night every Jew feels the kedushah, and the Sefer Torah is carried to everyone to kiss it and ask its forgiveness.

title.en: A double Shabbos and the Arvei Nachal's mashal

summary.en: The Rav explains that this Yom Kippur coincides with Shabbos, a 'double Shabbos' that the sefarim tie to the Gemara about keeping two Shabbosos. He then tells the Arvei Nachal's mashal of the king's servant whose two defenders, the king's children, are Shabbos and the Torah, and whom he must beg for forgiveness.

title.en: Honoring Shabbos with kedushah

summary.en: The Rav's message: refraining from melachah is not enough; Shabbos, the princess, must be honored with kedushah, not with newspapers, books or idle talk. He brings the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mother and explains that Hashem's rest included rest from speech, and that Shabbos is a day of song with the malachim.

title.en: The cleansing power and hope for Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Yoma that Yom Kippur alone only suspends grave sins, and the Taz that together with Shabbos it atones for them fully. He closes with the Chazal that when nations prepare for war it is a time to expect Moshiach, and with brachos.

catalogTitle: יכולים למצוא השי"ת בחודש אדר ובכל מאורעות הזמן

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Adar is the 'heel' of time, a month of garments and hiddenness, and that its avodah is to find Hashem's name hidden in the events of the world, as in the Megillah, and to laugh at the costumes of history.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the Tanya's question: if every Jewish soul is truly G-dly, how can Moshe Rabbeinu's generation be the 'head' and the final generations the 'heels'? He answers that the inner point is the same in all; only the garments differ. Since soul, time and place parallel each other, time too has a head, Nisan, the month of open miracles, and heels, Adar, the month of garments. The last generations, like the Torah's last parshiyos, live in hester within hester. The avodah of Adar is to find Hashem's name in the 'megillah' of world events, to know that 'the King' is Hashem, and to laugh at the costumes. He develops this through Yaakov's descent to Egypt, Mordechai and David sparing Shimi, rulers as puppets, the Maharal on the speed of the Purim miracle and Naftali's swiftness, ending with simcha within hester.

en: All Jewish souls are truly G-dly; the difference between the great early generations and the last ones lies only in how many garments cover the same inner point.
Like the soul, time has a head and heels: Nisan, the month of revealed miracles, is the head, and Adar, the furthest point from Nisan, is the heels, a month of garments.
The avodah of Adar is to search for Hashem's name in the world's events, in the news and in one's own experiences, just as the mekubalim found His name hidden in the Megillah.
One who knows that 'the King' means Hashem is not frightened by the costumes of history but laughs at them, and laughter is the trait of Adar.
The rulers of the world are like puppets moved by strings from above; what matters is not who sits in power but the King, Hashem.
Events that happen with great speed are a sign of Hashem's hand, as the Maharal says of the Purim miracle, and Adar, the month of Naftali, is a swift month.
The joy of Purim comes not from what one has but from seeing Hashem's name, so one can be b'simcha even within hester.

candidateTopics: Mordechai and the decree of Haman

title.en: The generations as one body: head and heels

summary.en: After a brief, garbled opening, the Rav describes the generations as one body, with Moshe Rabbeinu's generation the head and the generations before Moshiach the heels. He raises the Tanya's question of how souls that are truly G-dly can differ in level, and reads its answer of the son drawn from the father's mind.

title.en: Same inner point, different garments

summary.en: The Rav answers that the inner point of every Jew is the same in the head as in the heels; the difference is only how much physicality covers it. Like a fetus that needs nine months to form, Moshe Rabbeinu's soul came with few garments and the souls before Moshiach with many.

title.en: Nisan the head of time, Adar its heels

summary.en: Since place, time and soul parallel each other, the Rav shows that time too has a head, Nisan, 'rosh chodashim', and heels, Adar, the month furthest from Nisan. Nisan, from 'nes', is a month of open miracles, while Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is wrapped in garments.

title.en: The last generations and the Torah's last parshiyos

summary.en: The Rav compares the souls of the heels to the Torah's order: Bereishis corresponds to Moshe Rabbeinu, and today's souls to the last parshiyos, where there is no one to ask and Hashem says He will hide His face. In the heels there is a hester within hester, which the Ba'al Shem Tov spoke of.

title.en: Adar, Adar Sheini and Megillas Esther

summary.en: The Rav calls Adar a month of garments in which Hashem appears hidden. When the hester seems to end, a second Adar begins, hester upon hester. He brings the Kozhnitzer Maggid on the name 'Megillas Esther' and notes that Jews make a brachah on the miracles of a Megillah that seems to tell only ordinary events and never names Hashem.

title.en: Costumes, 'the King', and the hidden Name

summary.en: The Rav explains that all the events of the Megillah are miracles clothed in nature, and that the custom of dressing up teaches that garments mean nothing: Chazal say 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem. From Purim one leaves knowing that the hidden guidance is also His, and the mekubalim found His name in the Megillah's roshei teivos at its turning points.

title.en: Searching for Hashem in the world, and laughing

summary.en: The Rav says the avodah of Adar is to find Hashem's name in the 'megillah' of the world, where He peers through the cracks. A child is frightened by a man dressed as Haman, but one who sees Hashem's name laughs. Adar's organ is the spleen, the source of laughter, so its avodah is to laugh at the newspapers and commentators and to know that 'the King' is Hashem.

title.en: The claim against Europe's rabbis, and Yaakov's descent to Egypt

summary.en: The Rav takes up the claim that the rabbis and rebbes of Europe erred by not urging Jews toward Eretz Yisrael before the war. He answers from Yaakov Avinu: his going down to Egypt could look like a mistake, but it was a decree from Hashem, and Chazal say he would otherwise have been brought in iron chains. Instead of complaining 'my way is hidden', one should look through the cracks of the hester.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the complaints against Mordechai

summary.en: The Rav describes the Megillah's story unfolding over years. Mordechai cried out not to go to Achashverosh's feast, though everything there was kosher, yet many Jews went; later he refused to bow to Haman, and Jews blamed him for the decree.

title.en: Ish Yehudi and Ish Yemini: David and Shimi

summary.en: The Rav asks who really caused the decree and brings the Gemara on 'ish Yehudi … ish Yemini': Knesses Yisrael complains that David did not kill Shimi, from whom Mordechai descended. At the end of the Megillah it became clear that David's mercy was the cause of the rescue, because David saw Hashem's name even in Shimi's curse, and measure for measure he brought forth Mordechai, who revealed the hester.

title.en: Rulers as puppets and the 'Jewish question'

summary.en: The Rav says rulers are marionettes on strings from above, so it makes no difference who sits in the White House; it depends on the King. He notes that the whole world revolves around the Jews, that a progressive nation followed a leader set on 'solving the Jewish question', and tells of an old Jew angered at having to wait six hours after meat, explaining that the very existence of Jews proclaims morality and arouses hatred.

title.en: Hiding until the wrath passes; the Maharal on speed

summary.en: The Rav says the answer to the 'Jewish question' is 'chavi kim'at rega': go into your rooms, take your Gemara and Mishnayos and hide until the wrath passes, as Esther hid her origins. He then asks where the miracles of the Megillah are and brings the Maharal that they lie in the speed of the events, a sign of Hashem's hand, which he sees in his own times too.

title.en: Naftali, the swift tribe of Adar

summary.en: The Rav links Adar to the tribe of Naftali, whom Yaakov blessed as 'ayalah sheluchah', not for a particular quality but for swiftness, and brings Chazal's account of Naftali running to bring the deed. When Jews are low and Amalek high, things happen with Naftali's speed, and so even amid distress one must learn to laugh and be b'simcha.

title.en: Simcha within hester, and Adar leading to Nisan

summary.en: The Rav warns against losing hope when the redemption seems delayed, and says the joy of Purim comes from seeing Hashem's name, so it can exist even within hester; in simcha alone one may go to extremes. He closes by joining Adar to Nisan, 'to join redemption to redemption'.

catalogTitle: וטוב לב משתה תמיד - להודות לה' ולהתקרב אליו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the halachic standing of the Purim Katan seudah according to the Rema and the Acharonim, and shows how 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid' means thanking Hashem and drawing close to Him even in a time of hiddenness.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rema on Purim Katan: some say there is an obligation of mishteh v'simcha in Adar Rishon, the custom is otherwise, yet one should add a little to the meal, and 'a good heart is a constant feast.' He sets out the dispute behind it, with Tosfos holding that mishteh v'simcha belongs only to Adar Sheni, and brings the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer that a place or family saved by a miracle may make a day of thanks. He concludes that the Purim Katan seudah is a mitzvah, not a chiyuv, may be held at night, and lacks the halachos of seudas Purim. He then explains the leap month as the moon, Knesses Yisroel, catching up to the sun, and teaches that thanking Hashem in hester panim gives Him great nachas, and that Adar is a time for tefillah.

en: The Rema rules that although the custom is not to treat Adar Rishon as a day of mishteh v'simcha, one should add somewhat to the meal on Purim Katan, ending with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'.

According to the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer, a community or family that experienced a miracle may set a day of celebration, and the Rav argues that Purim Katan should be no less than such a private Purim.
The Rav concludes that the Purim Katan seudah is a mitzvah but not an obligation, may be held at night, and does not require the halachos of seudas Purim.
The leap month exists so that the lunar year can catch up with the solar year, which the Rav reads as Knesses Yisroel, the moon, returning to Hashem, the sun.
When Jews sit down to thank Hashem in a time of hester panim, without being commanded, it brings Him great nachas, and Adar is a time to pour out one's heart in tefillah.

title.en: The Rema's ruling and the custom

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Rema's words on Purim Katan, that some say there is an obligation of mishteh v'simcha but the custom is otherwise, and stresses that one does not rule against an established minhag.

title.en: A day of thanks for a private miracle

summary.en: The Rav brings the Magen Avraham and the Chasam Sofer that a community or family saved by a miracle may make a yearly day of celebration, sets out the dispute of the Rishonim on the Mishnah about Adar Rishon, and asks why Purim should be less than such a private day, since we are the descendants of those saved.

title.en: Tosfos and the nature of the seudah

summary.en: Following Tosfos, mishteh v'simcha as Mordechai's enactment belongs only to Adar Sheni and requires wine; the Rav explains that a seudah in Adar Rishon would instead be thanks for the miracle, without all the laws of seudas Purim, and mentions Rabbi Avraham of Ciechanow drinking wine to fulfil the mitzvah.

title.en: Why the Rema says 'a little more in the meal'

summary.en: The Rav analyzes the Rema's change of wording from 'mishteh v'simcha' to 'adding a little to the meal', showing that it follows the Magen Avraham's reasoning and does not uproot the custom, and explains 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid' as a meal with a glass of wine and l'chaim.

title.en: A seudah at night, on the day of the miracle

summary.en: The Rav asks whether a seudah that is a remembrance of the miracle may be held at night, and answers that it may; he discusses that such a remembrance belongs on the day the miracle happened, and suggests that this is the source of the custom to make a small seudah on the night of Purim Katan.

title.en: The leap month: the moon returns to the sun

summary.en: Bringing the tzaddikim that Adar Rishon is a month of teshuvah, the Rav explains the leap month as the lunar year catching up with the solar year: the sun is Hashem, the moon is Knesses Yisroel, which drifted away through sin; Purim Katan is linked to the 'small luminary', and its feast is the joy of Knesses Yisroel returning to Hashem.

title.en: The last month repairs the year

summary.en: The Rav explains that the last, added month can repair what was missed in the earlier months, brings the Midrash comparing Esther to the morning star at the end of the night, and describes the renewal it brings: a fresh acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, like a new creation.

title.en: An episode from the British Mandate

summary.en: After a stretch the ASR did not capture, the Rav tells of an episode in Eretz Yisroel under the British Mandate, connected to a planned public desecration of Shabbos; most details are unrecoverable.

title.en: L'chaim, and Haman's reckoning of Adar

summary.en: The Rav calls for l'chaim with wishes for health and the coming redemption, then turns to Haman, a master of calculations of times and lots, who rejoiced that his lot fell in Adar, the month of Moshe's passing, and connects his error to the intercalation of the year.

title.en: Untranscribed stretch

summary.en: About eight minutes of audio the ASR did not transcribe.

title.en: Seizing every chance to thank Hashem

summary.en: The Rav notes that some held the seudah should be by day, then teaches that a Jew should seize even the smallest occasion to thank Hashem, who is the same as for all earlier generations, and brings the Midrash that 'we will rejoice in Him' means rejoicing with Hashem rather than with the day.

title.en: The force of minhag and private Purims

summary.en: The Rav stresses that a minhag decides even in weighty matters, then discusses private Purims set by communities in Europe saved from decrees, which the Chasam Sofer discusses, and the possibility that the Men of the Great Assembly enacted mishteh v'simcha only for Adar Sheni.

title.en: No less than the Purim of Amsterdam

summary.en: The Rav asks why Purim Katan should be less than the private Purims of Cracow or Amsterdam, and concludes that making it a day of mishteh v'simcha is a mitzvah though not an obligation, so its seudah does not need the halachos of seudas Purim, like the joy of eating meat in the time of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: A gathering with l'chaim and blessings

summary.en: Returning to the Rema's wording, the Rav describes the custom: Jews sit together at a private gathering, sing, pour a glass of wine, say l'chaim and bless one another, which he calls 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'; it may be at night or whenever one wishes, since no halachos bind it.

title.en: Rejoicing in Hashem, not in the day

summary.en: The Rav asks what the Midrash adds by reading 'nagilah v'nismecha bo' as rejoicing with Hashem, and explains that one can rejoice with Hashem even when the time does not call for it; he then describes the descent through the generations to the lowest time, when Knesses Yisroel, the moon, is far from the sun in exile.

title.en: From 'shivisi' to 'tov lev mishteh tamid'

summary.en: The Rav notes that the halachos of Purim Katan are the last in Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, which opens with 'shivisi Hashem l'negdi tamid' and closes with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid'; in the twelfth month, in the darkness of hester panim when no salvation comes, Jews still make a seudah to thank Hashem, with emunah in the nights.

title.en: Uncommanded thanks and tefillah in Adar

summary.en: The Rav teaches that when Jews in hester panim sit down to thank Hashem without being commanded, Purim Katan can accomplish more than Purim itself, connecting this to 'yehei shmei rabba' and to Esther pleading before the king. He closes by calling Adar a time to pour out one's heart in tefillah for the geulah of Nissan.

catalogTitle: האור של מגילת אסתר יותר נעלה מאור של תורת משה (חתם סופר)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah has two faces, the level of Kesuvim all year and on Purim a light higher even than Toras Moshe, and that through it Klal Yisroel, even in its lowest state, is revealed as Hashem's kallah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that a Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, and with Esther's place among the prophetesses. He explains that certain parts of Torah have two faces: the Aseres HaDibros read with the upper or lower cantillation, and the song of David in Navi and in Tehillim. So too the Megillah: all year it is Kesuvim, but on Purim a higher world comes down and, as the Chasam Sofer writes, its light is greater than that of Toras Moshe. For this Esther had to be a prophetess. He then explains that Purim is for those who have fallen far: 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman means 'to His kallah', like a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place. 'Al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah'. He applies this to Purim Katan, to the small avodah of today, and ends with joy and brachos for the chosson and kallah.

en: A Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, because on Purim the Megillah rises above the level of Kesuvim.
Some parts of Torah have two faces, a higher and a lower level, such as the Aseres HaDibros with the upper and lower cantillation.
Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav says the greatness of the Megillah on Purim is higher than the light of Toras Moshe.
Purim belongs to the Jews who have fallen far; even there they remain Hashem's kallah.
The words 'al mikra megillah' in the bracha equal 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria.

candidateTopics: kesuvim and the levels of tanach

title.en: A Megillah among the Kesuvim; Esther the prophetess

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that a Megillah written among the other books of Kesuvim is not valid, and asks how this fits the bracha 'al mikra megillah'. He brings the Gemara's count of prophets and prophetesses, Rashi on why Daniel is not counted, and Esther's place among the prophetesses, and mentions how Haman's decree bound all Jews together.

title.en: Two faces in Torah; the Chasam Sofer on the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Aseres HaDibros read in public with the upper cantillation are on a higher level than when read alone, and that the song of David stands higher in Navi than in Tehillim. He brings the Yerushalmi that the Megillah will remain when other books are annulled, and the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's greatness is higher than the light of Toras Moshe.

title.en: The Megillah's new light on Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah is Kesuvim all year but on Purim receives a new light, which is why one written among the Kesuvim is invalid. To write it above the Kesuvim, Esther had to be a prophetess; he connects 'vatilbash Esther malchus' and the inner court of the king to the world where all Jews are bound together at the root of their souls.

title.en: Purim for the fallen; 'lechalosam' as His kallah

summary.en: The Rav says Purim is for those who have fallen far, and that the hidden love of Hashem, which many waters cannot extinguish, is revealed through the Megillah. He reads the Gemara's 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman as 'to His kallah', with a mashal of a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place to bring her back.

title.en: Esther cries out; 'al mikra megillah' as chosson v'kallah

summary.en: The Rav describes Esther crying out to Hashem from the lowest place, and says the joy of Purim is that Jews know that in whatever state they are, even outside the camp, they are Hashem's kallah. Therefore the bracha 'al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria.

title.en: Purim Katan and the heavenly yeshiva

summary.en: The Rav explains that although the Megillah is read in the second Adar, the joy belongs to Purim Katan too, and that in Heaven there is a yeshiva that follows Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Yosi, where the Megillah is read today. He adds that on Purim a Jew may enter the heichal of whichever tanna he wishes, and that a small avodah of today, such as negel vasser, is precious in Heaven.

title.en: Joy of chosson and kallah; brachos

summary.en: The Rav says Jews gather to strengthen the emunah that they are Hashem's kallah, connects 'vaye'ehav hamelech es Esther' to the joy of chosson and kallah, and blesses the chosson, kallah and families. He closes with 'tov lev mishteh tamid' and the hope that the joy may help bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: The מקוה of יו”כ Reveals the Essence of Good in Every Yid

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yom Kippur, the fortieth day of teshuvah, is a mikveh in time in which every Jew reaches the hidden point of good from Avraham Avinu in his heart, and Hashem Himself cleanses him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the last Mishnah of Yoma: Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time, and Hashem Himself is the mikveh. He builds on the number forty: an embryo is formed in forty days, and the Chiddushei HaRim teaches that in every Jew's heart there is one hidden point, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, that evil never reaches, which is why Hashem is called 'Magen Avraham'. This explains the Rambam on a person coerced to say 'I want', and why a sinner receives only thirty-nine lashes, Adam received thirty-nine curses, and the generation of the desert was spared in the fortieth year. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul end on Yom Kippur, the fortieth se'ah of the mikveh, when a Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his own heart. Through the Yismach Moshe's parable of a stained suit he teaches that Hashem removes what our teshuvah cannot, and he closes that Yom Kippur is a joyous day to be cherished.

en: Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time, and on it Hashem Himself is the mikveh who cleanses a Jew of his sins.
Following the Chiddushei HaRim, every Jew has one hidden point in his heart, inherited from Avraham Avinu, that evil cannot reach, and there he wants to be a tzaddik.
A sinner receives thirty-nine lashes rather than forty because his fortieth point never agreed to the sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul culminate on Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, when the mikveh of forty se'ah is complete and a Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his heart.
A Jew must do teshuvah as far as he can, and Hashem removes the stains he cannot remove himself.
Yom Kippur is an awesome day but also a joyous one, and one should cherish every minute of it rather than count the hours until the fast ends.

title.en: Yom Kippur as a mikveh, and the number forty

summary.en: The Rav opens with the last Mishnah of Yoma, 'Ashreichem Yisrael' and 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem', and explains that Yom Kippur is a mikveh made of time in which Hashem Himself cleanses a Jew. He then introduces the forty days in which an embryo is formed, bringing the Gemara in Berachos and Rashi on the forty days of the Mabul.

title.en: The hidden point of Avraham in every heart

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah says forty lashes while only thirty-nine are given, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim on 'Magen Avraham': in every Jew there is a hidden point from Avraham Avinu that evil cannot reach. With this he explains the Rambam on a person who is beaten until he says 'I want' to bring his korban.

title.en: Thirty-nine lashes, curses and melachos

summary.en: The Rav answers that a sinner receives only thirty-nine lashes because his fortieth point protested the sin. He applies the same idea to the thirty-nine curses after the sin of Adam, which are the source of the thirty-nine melachos forbidden on Shabbos, and to the generation of the desert who were all spared in the fortieth year.

title.en: The fortieth day and the inner Holy of Holies

summary.en: The Rav counts the forty days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, when the Satan has no power. As the Kohen Gadol enters the Holy of Holies, every Jew enters the Holy of Holies in his heart, especially at Ne'ilah, where no angel and no Satan can enter.

title.en: The fortieth se'ah completes the mikveh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that a kosher mikveh needs forty se'ah: each day of Elul adds a se'ah, and on Yom Kippur the mikveh is complete. The climax of the Avodah recited in Musaf is the Kohen Gadol's entry into the Holy of Holies, and so too every Jew reaches his pure yetzer tov and resolves to be good for the coming year.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe's parable of the stained suit

summary.en: The Rav tells the Yismach Moshe's parable of a man whose suit for an audience with the king was stained with tar, which only an expert could fully clean. Teshuvah cannot remove every stain, he explains, but Hashem is the expert who does the rest, as in the case of someone who cannot recall whom he wronged; he urges saying at least the forgiveness lines of Tefillah Zakah.

title.en: Yom Kippur, an awesome and joyous day

summary.en: The Rav says Yom Kippur is awesome but also a happy day: in place of physical pleasures it has five tefillos full of delight, in which Hashem speaks back to the Jew and says He erases his sins like a cloud. He criticizes those who watch the clock waiting to eat; one should hold on to every minute.

title.en: Chaim and Yankel, and closing brachos

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Chaim, who enjoys Yom Kippur, with Yankel, who keeps checking his watch; both eat at the same time, but Yankel spoiled his Yom Kippur, as the Yesod v'Shoresh HaAvodah writes. He sums up that one must do teshuvah yet feel fortunate to have Yom Kippur, and closes with brachos for a good inscription and the Geulah.

catalogTitle: סעודת "טוב להודות לה'"

oneLiner.en: At a Purim Katan seudah the Rav explains why the fourteenth of Adar I still calls for a commemoration of the miracle, and why Purim's high light needs to be repeated and strengthened, ending with 'Tov lehodos laShem', the good of praising Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that Adar I and Adar II differ only in Megillah reading and gifts to the poor, and the dispute whether feasting is required on Adar I, which the Rema settles with 'increase the meal a little'. With the Magen Avraham's rule on commemorating a miracle, he asks how such a commemoration could be pushed off entirely. He brings the Chasam Sofer, who says the Torah-level duty to commemorate a miracle is met in Adar I by refraining from eulogy and fasting, and questions it. He weighs zerizus against doing a mitzvah in its finest way, and explains 'igeres haPurim hashenis'. From Pharaoh's doubled dream and the Maharal he explains that Purim's light comes from so high that it must be repeated to stay in the world, and that a leap year needs two Purims. He closes with 'Tov lehodos laShem' and brachos.

en: According to the Rav, beyond the Purim that Mordechai and Esther instituted, there is a general duty, as the Magen Avraham writes, to commemorate a miracle, and this is why something of Purim remains on Adar I.
The Rav explains the Rema's 'increase the meal a little' as adding wine, since the Purim seudah requires wine while a general commemoration of a miracle does not.

The Rav questions the Chasam Sofer's view that refraining from eulogy and fasting fulfils the commemoration, since a commemoration must be a positive act, and on an ordinary day too there is no eulogy or fast.
Purim's miracle came from so high a place, beyond nature and beyond understanding, that its light tends to rise back up, so it must be held and strengthened by repetition.
This repetition, the Rav suggests, is behind reading the Megillah at night and again by day, and behind Esther's making two feasts.
In a leap year the lowliness of the thirteenth month is deeper still, so two Purims are needed, Purim Katan together with the great Purim.
The Purim Katan seudah is an expression of 'Tov lehodos laShem': it is good to praise Hashem, and a person who has a taste in davening finds that all of his life changes.

title.en: Feasting on Adar I and the Rema

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah on Adar I and II and the dispute over feasting on Adar I, settled by the Rema. With the Magen Avraham's rule on commemorating a miracle, he asks how Adar I can be left empty, and explains the Rema's 'increase a little' as adding wine.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer and the Rav's question

summary.en: The Rav brings a Chasam Sofer close to what he once said: commemorating a miracle is a Torah duty, fulfilled in Adar I by refraining from eulogy and fasting. He then asks how refraining can be a commemoration, when a positive act is needed.

title.en: Zerizus, mitzvah min hamuvchar and 'hashenis'

summary.en: The Rav suggests the dispute may follow Rav Nachman and Rava on Hallel, then weighs zerizus against a mitzvah in its finest form, with the Chacham Tzvi and the Terumas HaDeshen. He explains how zerizus applies to Purim and how 'igeres haPurim hashenis' refers to reading the Megillah a second time.

title.en: Purim's high light must be repeated

summary.en: From a case of mistaken Kiddush the Rav shows that Adar I holds some holiness of Purim. With Pharaoh's doubled dream and the Maharal he explains that Purim's light comes from so high that it must be strengthened by repetition, as in reading the Megillah twice and Esther's two feasts.

title.en: Two Purims, 'Tov lehodos' and brachos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the thirteenth month is a deeper darkness that needs a double Purim, and that the seudah is a commemoration and a preparation for the next Purim. He speaks on 'Tov lehodos laShem' and the taste of good davening, and closes with brachos for salvation and the final redemption.

catalogTitle: עיקר הפורים הוא בעקבתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the main Purim has not yet come: it is the last Purim before Moshiach, in the time of greatest hiddenness, and from Purim Katan a Jew draws the strength not to be afraid.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rema that one should add a little feasting on Purim Katan, and with the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi that the main Purim is in the first Adar, which is ruled so in a heichal in Heaven, from where light descends today. He then explains why reading the Megillah 'backwards' does not fulfil the mitzvah: Purim is not only a past event, since the main Purim, the complete wiping out of Amalek, comes in the hiddenness before Moshiach. He brings the Sfas Emes that another Purim may precede the third Beis Hamikdash, and describes Haman's kelipah as fear. He connects the Babylon of his day and Achashverosh's rule 'by himself' to that last Purim, tells how Chizkiyahu slept calmly on Pesach night, and brings Mordechai and the children's pesukim against fear. He ends with Purim Katan as the last siman of Orach Chaim, accepting Torah anew, and an appeal for a hachnasas orchim.

en: According to the Rav, the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi that Purim belongs in the first Adar is upheld in a heichal in Heaven, and its light reaches us on Purim Katan.
Unlike Pesach and Shavuos, the main Purim has not yet happened: the full wiping out of Amalek comes in the hiddenness before Moshiach.
The closer to the end of days, the greater the hiddenness, and therefore the greater the Purim; in every generation Amalek wages a new war, and so there is a new Purim.
Haman's kelipah is fear: he did nothing but cast fear on the Jews, and the Megillah teaches not to be overcome by that fear.
The Rav says one should say every day, especially nowadays, the three pesukim the children told Mordechai, which teach not to fear.
The laws of Purim Katan are the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, matching Adar as the last month and the time before Moshiach.

title.en: Purim Katan and the heichal in Heaven

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rema on feasting on Purim Katan and the Gemara's dispute whether Purim belongs in the first or second Adar. He explains that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosi's view is ruled in a heichal in Heaven, from where light comes down today, and introduces the sefarim's reading of 'one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled his obligation'.

title.en: The main Purim is still to come

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Purim with Pesach and Shavuos: their events are past and their light returns each year, but the main Purim, the complete wiping out of Amalek, has not yet been. He ties Purim to the hiddenness of 'haster astir', which the Torah places at the end of days, and explains that every generation has a new war with Amalek and so a new Purim.

title.en: A Purim before the third Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that just as the Purim miracle gave the Jews the uplift to build the second Beis Hamikdash, there may be another such miracle before Moshiach. On this he explains 'reading the Megillah backwards': one who thinks Purim is only past misses that the real Purim is just before Moshiach, and he brings the Ya'avetz on the miracle of Jewish survival in exile.

title.en: Haman's fear and the Babylon of today

summary.en: The Rav describes Haman's kelipah as fear and says Amalek in this generation is clothed in Babylon, whose ruler claims to be Nebuchadnezzar and threatens the Jews. He brings the Rashab's writings on the seventy nations' ministering angels, the passuk 'kol kli yutzar alayich lo yitzlach', and the Shabbos zemer's request that Babylon too be crushed.

title.en: The first petichta and a king 'by himself'

summary.en: The Rav asks why the first petichta of the Midrash on the Megillah speaks of cutting off Babylon, and answers that the last Purim before Moshiach is the Purim of 'v'hikrati l'Vavel'. In a lighter Purim vein he explains Achashverosh as a king who ruled 'by himself', chosen by Hashem and not by the people, compares it to the Maharal on the giving of the Torah, and applies it to the American president of his day.

title.en: Chizkiyahu's sleep and the children's pesukim

summary.en: The Rav tells how Chizkiyahu slept calmly on Pesach night while Sancheriv's army surrounded Yerushalayim, a sign of bitachon. He explains that Purim's 'v'nahafoch' turns fear back onto the enemy, brings 'tipol aleihem eimasa vafachad' and the passuk about Yishmael, and tells how Mordechai was encouraged by the pesukim the children told him, which the Rav says one should say daily.

title.en: The last siman of Orach Chaim

summary.en: The Rav notes that the laws of Purim Katan are the last siman of Orach Chaim, 697, and brings the Ya'avetz that the Mechaber numbered the simanim with ruach hakodesh. He offers gematrias on the number and calls for a renewed acceptance of Torah, as in 'kiymu v'kiblu'.

title.en: Hachnasas orchim and closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav praises a hachnasas orchim founded by Rabbi Boruch Halberstam in Boro Park and asks the listeners to help it. He closes with the Rema's last halacha in Orach Chaim on feasting on Purim Katan and a brachah for the full wiping out of Amalek and the building of the third Beis Hamikdash.

catalogTitle: אביגיל מלכת פורים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the Gemara tells the story of Avigail in the middle of the laws of Purim: Avigail, whose name equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, is the aspect of Purim, the beginning of the kingdom of the house of David, which is completed through Bas Sheva and Pesach.

abstract.en: The Rav retells how Avigail stopped David from killing Naval, telling him 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah', which the Gemara counts as prophecy, hinting at Bas Sheva. He asks what kind of prophecy that is, and why the story stands in the Purim sugya. Bringing the Gemara that Mordechai's yom tov was not accepted, he says that the Megillah speaks on two levels, the historical Achashverosh and the King, Hashem, and of the final war with Amalek; the full yom tov still waits. He explains the Bas Sheva episode: David knew she was his zivug, and the kingdom of David must come through hidden, talked-about ways so the Satan will not notice. Avigail, from the same root, saw that David thought Moshiach would come from her and told him: not through me. Avigail equals Esther Hamalkah; Purim is the start of the kingdom, completed at Pesach. He closes with the simcha of Purim Katan.

en: The Gemara counts Avigail's words 'lo sihyeh zos lecha lefukah' as prophecy, because they hinted at the episode of Bas Sheva.
The Megillah speaks on two levels: the historical Achashverosh, and the King, Hashem, and the final war with Amalek; therefore the yom tov Mordechai wanted was not yet accepted.
The kingdom of the house of David comes through hidden ways that cause people to talk, so that the Satan will not realize where it is coming from; this is why David acted as he did with Bas Sheva.
Avigail understood that David thought Moshiach would come from her, and told him that the kingdom would come through Bas Sheva and not through her.
Avigail is the aspect of Purim and of Esther; Purim is the beginning of the kingdom of the house of David and of the redemption, which continues to Pesach.
On Purim Katan there is no Megillah, mishloach manos or matanos la'evyonim, but the mitzvah of simcha applies.

summary.en: The Rav explains that David deliberately caused people to talk, yet still needed atonement, like one who fasts on Shabbos and needs a fast for that fast, or the nazir who brings a chatas. He then explains that David understood Avigail was his zivug, from the same root as Bas Sheva.

title.en: Hod, Purim to Pesach, and Avigail's answer

summary.en: The Rav explains that the kingdom comes from the aspect of hod, that Purim is the beginning of the kingdom of David and leads to Pesach, and that Avigail told David: not through me, the kingdom will come from Bas Sheva. He adds that Purim prepares the three mitzvos of a king, Amalek and the Beis Hamikdash.

summary.en: The Rav brings that Avigail the wife of David equals Esther Hamalkah in gematria, and that a missing yud in her name shows that malchus is missing. He explains that Avigail is the aspect of Purim, and connects the first place each name appears in the pesukim.

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Purim Katan only the mitzvah of simcha remains, ties it to the end of the Shulchan Aruch and to Haman's lot falling in the first Adar, and closes with a brachah to be together in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: Subordinating Ourselves to Hashem on these Holy Days

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that bowing down on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur is total subordination to Hashem as King, possible outside the Beis HaMikdash only because these ten days are the Beis HaMikdash in time, and that when a Jew bows, all of creation bows with him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the greatness of Yom Kippur, the Shabbos of all Shabbosim, when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim and every Jew rises to the level of the angels. Leaving the main themes to the boys' own rebbeim, he takes one small custom: falling prostrate in the davening. Bowing means surrendering one's existence before the King, and the Ba'al HaTanya writes that this is possible only in the Beis HaMikdash, the place of Malchus. Why then do we bow on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur? Using the Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of place, time and soul, the Rav explains that the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time: the King comes to us. He then describes the world before Adam's sin, Adam's call to all creatures to bow, and the power of a Jew's bowing and teshuvah to move all creation, ending with the dog's song in Perek Shirah.

en: Hishtachavayah, falling prostrate, means total subordination to Hashem as King, to the point of surrendering one's own existence.
Such total subordination belongs to the Beis HaMikdash, the place of Malchus, so outside it bowing would not be real.
The ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time, so on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to us and we may bow wherever we are.
On these days we ask Hashem to bring back the world as it was before Adam's sin, when all creation accepted His kingship.
A Jew's teshuvah and bowing move the whole creation, because all of creation is connected with the Jewish people.

summary.en: The Rav describes Yom Kippur as the Shabbos of all Shabbosim, a day like the World to Come when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim on behalf of all Jews. He lists its main themes, fasting, teshuvah, vidui and appeasing others, and says he will instead explain one small custom of the day.

title.en: Bowing before the King

summary.en: The Rav asks what the falling prostrate of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur means, and explains that in these days, when Hashem is near, His kingship is present and bowing is total self-nullification before the King. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya that such bowing is possible only in the Beis HaMikdash, and asks why we bow on these days.

title.en: The Beis HaMikdash in time

summary.en: Using the Sefer Yetzirah's teaching that creation is made in place, time and soul, the Rav explains that Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the calendar and the ten days of teshuvah are the Beis HaMikdash in time. Malchus comes to us, which is why we bow, why there is no mitzvah to go up to Yerushalayim on Yom Kippur, and why the chazzan calls out HaMelech from where he stands.

title.en: Adam's world and the window-shade string

summary.en: The Rav describes the world at Adam's creation, when everything accepted Hashem's kingship, which we ask to restore on these days. He tells of Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz holding a window-shade string during Shemoneh Esrei of Rosh Hashanah, and brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Adam called all creatures to bow, and they did.

title.en: The power of a Jew's teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav teaches that a Jew does not realize how powerful he is: his teshuvah moves all creatures and other Jews far away, because everything is connected to the Jewish people, as the passuk says everything was put under Adam's feet. When he bows on Yom Kippur and declares he has no wish but Hashem's, all creation bows with him, like one button lighting a whole tower.

title.en: The dog's song in Perek Shirah

summary.en: The Rav brings Perek Shirah, where every creature has a passuk of song, and asks why the dog says the same words Adam used to call creation to bow. He explains why the dog is a term of contempt: it is not independent and is happy with a substitute master, while true freedom is to serve Hashem alone. The recording cuts off as he returns to Adam's call.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ב - עושים שמחה כדי לזכור הנס

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why, although the custom is not to make a full feast on Purim Katan, a Jew should still rejoice that day: the miracle must be remembered, and on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rema's ruling on Purim Katan: some hold one must make a feast, the custom is not so, yet one should add somewhat to the meal, for 'a good heart is a constant feast'. He brings the Magen Avraham that every miracle obligates a yearly celebration, learned by kal vachomer from Hallel, and argues that by 'ein maavirin al hamitzvos' and 'zichru nifle'osav' it should belong to the first Adar. The Anshei Knesses HaGedolah set Purim in the second Adar, but the first still carries the mitzvah of remembering. Purim has two laws, the feast for the miracle and the wine instituted by Mordechai and Esther, which Purim Katan lacks. Finally he explains that on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, as Boaz's 'vayitav libo' refers to Torah study, so a Jew should rejoice on Purim Katan.

en: The Rema writes that some obligate a feast on Purim Katan and the custom is not so, yet one should add somewhat to the meal, since 'a good heart is a constant feast'.
According to the Magen Avraham, every miracle that happens to Jews obligates a yearly celebration, learned by kal vachomer from the Gemara's reasoning about saying Hallel.
Because of 'ein maavirin al hamitzvos' and the duty to remember Hashem's wonders within the year, the celebration of the miracle seemingly belongs on Purim Katan in the first Adar.

Purim has two separate laws: a feast to celebrate the miracle, and drinking wine as a remembrance, instituted by Mordechai and Esther because the miracle came through wine; the second does not apply to Purim Katan.
On Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, and a Jew cannot fail to rejoice over this on Purim Katan as well.
The simcha of Torah is not tied to a set day, so the custom of not making a feast on Purim Katan does not exclude rejoicing in the Torah on that day.

title.en: Remembering the miracle and the two laws of Purim

summary.en: The Rav compares the duty of 'zichru nifle'osav' to reading Parshas Zachor every year so that it is not forgotten, which would seemingly require a feast on Purim Katan. He then distinguishes two laws of Purim, the feast for the miracle and the wine instituted by Mordechai and Esther, and uses this to explain the Rema's wording.

title.en: Purim Katan and the joy of accepting the Torah

summary.en: The Rav asks what Purim Katan is and answers that on Purim the Jews accepted the Torah with love, a joy no Jew can postpone. He brings Boaz's 'vayitav libo', which the Gemara explains as Torah study, and concludes that rejoicing in the Torah belongs to every day and surely to Purim Katan, ending with a wish for joy in Heaven and the coming of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: תש"ס - אפשר כשיבא משיח יהיה פורים באדר ראשון

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, following the Chasam Sofer, that placing Purim next to Nissan is a segulah for salvation needed in galus, and suggests that when Moshiach comes Purim of a leap year may move to Adar Rishon, the month that repairs the diminished moon.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Yerushalmi that Adar Rishon is an addition and Adar Sheni the main month, and then brings the Gemara's dispute over which Adar of a leap year holds Purim: Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi argues from 'one does not pass over mitzvos', Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from joining redemption to redemption. He asks what lies behind the second reason, which Rashi gives no verse for. From the Chasam Sofer's account of how Haman and the Sanhedrin calculated the year, he concludes that joining the redemptions is a segulah for salvation, not a halacha. In galus Jews need that segulah like bread; when Moshiach comes it will no longer be needed, so Purim may then fall in Adar Rishon. He explains the name Purim Katan through the small luminary and the moon's diminution, which Adar Rishon repairs, and closes with the humility of Shaul, Mordechai and Esther.

en: Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi places Purim of a leap year in the first Adar because one does not pass over mitzvos; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel places it in the second to join the redemption of Adar to that of Nissan, and the practice follows him.
From the Chasam Sofer's account of Haman's calculation the Rav concludes that joining redemption to redemption is a segulah for salvation, neither a Torah law nor a rabbinic one.
In galus Jews need Purim's power of salvation like bread, so the Sages fixed it in the second Adar; when Moshiach comes that need falls away and Purim may move to Adar Rishon.
The name Purim Katan points to the small luminary: Adar Rishon is the month that fills in the moon's diminution and reconciles Kenesses Yisrael with Hashem.
Humility brings kingship and salvation: Binyamin, Shaul and Mordechai had lowliness in themselves, and Esther, like the moon, had nothing of her own.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: Haman's calculation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's derush: Haman picked a year that should have been a leap year so his Adar would be far from Nissan, and the Sanhedrin countered by making it a plain year. From this he proves that joining redemption to redemption is a segulah, which the Sages kept because the days are remembered and re-enacted.

title.en: When Moshiach comes: Purim in Adar Rishon

summary.en: The Rav explains that in galus Jews need Purim's salvation like bread, against the power of Achashverosh, through the power of Mordechai and against Haman. When Moshiach comes it will only be a remembrance, so only the reason of not passing over mitzvos remains, and he suggests Purim of a leap year will then be in Adar Rishon.

title.en: Purim Katan and the diminished moon

summary.en: The Rav asks why the day is called Purim Katan and not Purim Rishon, and answers that Adar Rishon repairs the moon's diminution, the root of a chain of jealousies through history. Esther is the moon, and he ends with a brachah that in the merit of Purim Katan every Jew should long to reconcile with Hashem.

title.en: Lowliness brings kingship and redemption

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who has lowliness in himself merits kingship: Binyamin, Shaul, who did not reveal his kingship, and Mordechai, of whom it is said that Hashem stands at the right of the poor. Esther, like the moon, had nothing of her own, and the redemption came through people of true humility, upon whom Hashem looks.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ו - שמחים בנקודה קטנה שבתוך יהודי

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that on Purim Jews rejoice with the small hidden point in every Jew, the root that milah binds without da'as and from which mesiras nefesh comes.

abstract.en: The recording opens near the end of the seudah of Purim Katan. The Rav notes that the seudah is not obligatory by law, yet Jews rejoice with the Ribono shel Olam and His miracles, fulfilling the Rema's closing words in Shulchan Aruch. He then explains matanos la'evyonim through the saying that true poverty is poverty in da'as. He contrasts Amalek, the worst klipah, with milah, the covenant of Avraham Avinu, and asks why milah is not delayed until the child can do it with intent. His answer: precisely without da'as the infant is bound to the hidden root of the Jewish people. On Purim one rejoices with this hidden point, the love one does not even feel. Milah, without da'as, and tefillin, which demand constant da'as, belong together, and Purim joins them. From the root above da'as comes mesiras nefesh, which Hashem's decree drew out of Mordechai, who would not bow.

en: Although the seudah of Purim Katan is not obligatory, rejoicing with the Ribono shel Olam fulfils the Rema's closing words in Shulchan Aruch.
Milah is done at eight days, without da'as, and precisely so it binds the child to the hidden root of Avraham Avinu and of the Jewish people.
On Purim one rejoices with the hidden point in every Jew, the concealed love one does not even feel.
Milah, without da'as, and tefillin, which require da'as, are bound together, and Purim, with 'sasson' as milah and 'yekar' as tefillin, unites them.
A Jew's mesiras nefesh comes from the root above da'as, and the decree to bow to Haman was there to draw it out of Mordechai.

catalogTitle: The Avodah of the Day - Connect Yourself to the Essence of Your נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yom Kippur is the fortieth, innermost level of the Jewish soul, the yechidah, where every Jew truly wants to serve Hashem and all Jews are one, and from this he explains why appeasing others, malkus and mikveh on Erev Yom Kippur share one siman in the Shulchan Aruch.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why the Shulchan Aruch puts three Erev Yom Kippur practices in one siman: appeasing anyone one has wronged, receiving malkus, and immersing in the mikveh. He brings the Noam Elimelech on an upper world of Klal Yisrael, the level of yechidah where all souls are fused as one and no blemish reaches. He then brings the Ramban that the forty lashes match the forty stages of a child's formation, asks why only thirty-nine are given, and answers with the Rambam on compelled consent: the innermost fortieth level never sinned. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul form the year, and Yom Kippur, the fortieth, is when the yechidah surfaces. Yom Kippur is also the mikveh of Klal Yisrael. He ends with the Midrash of the tailor who paid twelve dinarim for a fish, showing love of Hashem that brings forgiveness.

en: Appeasing others, malkus and tevilah on Erev Yom Kippur appear together in one siman of the Shulchan Aruch, so there must be a link between them.
According to the Rav, the innermost level of the soul, the yechidah, is where all Jews are fused into one soul and where no sin reaches.
Only thirty-nine lashes are given because the fortieth, innermost stage of a person was never blemished by the sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur form the coming year, and Yom Kippur is the fortieth day, when the yechidah comes to the surface.
Yom Kippur is the mikveh of Klal Yisrael, the fortieth se'ah, so any quarrel left unresolved is a chatzitzah between one Jew and another.
The tailor who paid twelve dinarim for a fish showed his love of Hashem, and that love is itself the proof that he will be forgiven.

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that the forty lashes correspond to the forty stages of a child's formation, and asks why only thirty-nine are given. He answers with the Rambam on coercing someone until he says 'I want': deep down every Jew wants to serve Hashem, so the innermost fortieth stage was never blemished.

title.en: Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, and the yechidah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul form the year like the forty days of a child's formation, and Yom Kippur is the fortieth, when the soul's cry of 'I want' surfaces. He recalls a Rebbe teaching the five parts of the soul and says the aim of Yom Kippur is to consciously meet one's yechidah, which is also why it is a day of unity and of appeasing others.

title.en: Yom Kippur as the mikveh of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav brings the end of Mishnah Yoma, 'Mikveh Yisrael Hashem', and explains that each day of the forty adds a se'ah until Yom Kippur completes the mikveh. This explains the Kohen Gadol's immersions and our tevilah on Erev Yom Kippur, and ties all three practices of the siman to unity, since a quarrel is a chatzitzah.

title.en: The Midrash of the tailor and the fish

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash brought by the Tur: a Jewish tailor outbid the governor's servant and paid twelve dinarim for the only fish on Erev Yom Kippur. Summoned by the governor, he explained that Jews rejoice with fine food on Erev Yom Kippur, and the governor let him go.

title.en: Love of Hashem as the proof of forgiveness

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Midrash stresses the price and calls the tailor's words a proof. Comparing it to paying a high price for an esrog, he explains that spending beyond worth expresses love of Hashem, and since Hashem returns love, it proves He will forgive. He closes with the Ba'al Shem Tov's three loves and a call for love of Torah and of Jews in a year he expects to be momentous.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין "ואין נוהגין כן וכו' וטוב לב משתה תמיד" (סיום שו”ע או”ח רמ"א)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Rema's closing words on Purim Katan, why he tells us to eat a little more at a meal though the custom does not follow the Ran, and how 'vetov lev mishteh tamid' lets one satisfy the stringent view without breaking the minhag.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim, where the Rema brings the Ran's view that Purim Katan requires feasting, notes that the custom follows Tosfos, yet says to eat a little more 'to satisfy the stringent', closing with 'vetov lev mishteh tamid'. Since the Rema guards every minhag, why add this? The Rav brings the Magen Avraham that one who experienced a miracle should make that day a yom tov, which the Chasam Sofer derives from the Gemara's kal vachomer about Hallel, and the Magen Avraham that a yahrzeit is kept in both Adars. Purim's own mishteh is a special din tied to wine, because the miracle came through wine. So even Tosfos agrees one should rejoice on Purim Katan; the dispute is only about wine. The Rema's answer is that Jews always say l'chaim. The Rav closes with Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman.

en: The Rav says the Rema guards every minhag, so his instruction to eat a little more on Purim Katan, against the custom he himself records, needs an explanation.
According to the Magen Avraham, anyone who experiences a miracle should make that day a yom tov, as with Purim Krakow, and the Chasam Sofer calls this a mitzvah learned by kal vachomer from Pesach.
The mishteh of Purim is not the general din of celebrating a miracle but a special halachah requiring wine, because the Purim miracle came about through wine.
Even Tosfos agrees one should rejoice on Purim Katan by the Magen Avraham's din; the difference is that only by the Ran's view must one drink wine.

The Rema's closing words 'vetov lev mishteh tamid' show how to satisfy the stringent view: Jews always say l'chaim at a gathering, so drinking a little wine does not look like going against the minhag.
Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Haman whose family became Jews through the Purim miracle, had special reason for joy, which is why his son taught 'mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha'.

summary.en: The Rav reads the last siman of Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim on the 14th and 15th of Adar Rishon, the Mishnah that the two Adars differ only in Megillah and gifts to the poor, and the Rema's gloss ending with 'vetov lev mishteh tamid'. He says every word of the Rema is ruach hakodesh and deserves closer thought.

title.en: The Rema's strictness about minhag

summary.en: The Rav lays out the dispute between the Ran, who requires feasting on Purim Katan, and Tosfos, whom the custom follows. He shows the Rema's zeal for minhag with the example of shevarim-teruah blown in two breaths, and asks why the Rema then tells us to eat a little more at a meal.

title.en: A private Purim and a yahrzeit in Adar

summary.en: The Rav brings the Magen Avraham that a community or individual who experienced a miracle should make that day a yom tov, like Purim Krakow, and the Chasam Sofer who derives this mitzvah from the Gemara's kal vachomer about Hallel. He then brings the Magen Avraham that a yahrzeit is kept in both Adars, since only the Megillah is limited to the second Adar by the word 'hasheinis'.

title.en: Why Purim's feast needs wine

summary.en: The Rav explains the Ran's view that Purim Katan requires a feast, and asks why Chanukah has no din of mishteh vesimcha despite the kal vachomer. He answers that the mishteh of Purim is a special din, a remembrance of a miracle that came through wine, so by the Ran one must drink wine on Purim Katan too.

title.en: Even Tosfos agrees to rejoice

summary.en: The Rav asks why Tosfos does not require rejoicing on Purim Katan by the Magen Avraham's din, and answers that Tosfos too would agree to that. The difference is that a self-made yom tov like Purim Krakow can be celebrated in any way, even a parade, while Purim Gadol has halachos from Chazal that require wine.

title.en: Rereading the Rema: a l'chaim

summary.en: The Rav rereads the Rema phrase by phrase and points to the change of wording from 'mishteh vesimcha' to 'yarbeh ketzas biseudah'. He asks how a meal without wine satisfies the stringent view, and answers from 'vetov lev mishteh tamid': Jews always say l'chaim with a little wine, so one fulfills the Ran's view without visibly going against the minhag.

title.en: Wine or any strong drink?

summary.en: The Rav wonders whether the Purim drinking must be wine or any intoxicating drink, since the custom is to drink bronfen. He notes that wine is named at Vashti's feast while Esther's feasts mention only 'mishteh', contrasts kiddush where wine is required, mentions Rabbi Avraham of Tshechanov drinking a revi'is of wine on Purim, and remarks that bronfen is a newer drink.

title.en: Haman's descendant and the joy of Adar

summary.en: Short of time, the Rav brings the Gemara that 'mishenichnas Adar marbin besimcha' was said by Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas. From the Gemara that Haman's descendants taught Torah in Bnei Brak, he identifies Rav Shmuel bar Shilas as a descendant of Haman who would not have been a Jew without the Purim miracle, and so had special joy in Adar; he closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: סעודת פורים קטן

oneLiner.en: On Purim Katan the Rav explains, following the Chasam Sofer, that the joy of Purim stands on its own, and shows through the image of the Megillah as a kallah why that joy can join the joy of a chasan and kallah.

abstract.en: The opening of the recording is lost. When the speech becomes clear, the Rav brings the Chasam Sofer: rejoicing over a miracle, like the song sung over the redemption of Pesach, is itself an obligation, but the Torah gives no details, so the Sages set the seudah, matanos la'evyonim and mishloach manos. The joy itself, he says, is the deeper layer, and the Chasam Sofer holds that the seudah is not the only way to fulfill it. This, he explains, is the reason of the Yerushalmi that a Purim seudah falling on Shabbos is moved to Sunday: two joys are not mixed. That raises a question about joining a wedding's joy with Purim. The Rav answers with the passuk that Hashem does not reject Israel even in exile, the mashal of a king who goes to his kallah even in a disgraceful place, and Rashi's teaching that the twenty-four books are like a kallah's adornments. Megillas Esther became a kallah, so its joy is a kallah's joy, and there is no contradiction. He closes with a brachah for Yerushalayim.

en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that the joy over the Purim miracle is an obligation in its own right, while the Sages only set its details: the seudah, gifts to the poor and mishloach manos.
The Rav says this is the reason of the Yerushalmi that a Purim seudah falling on Shabbos is made on Sunday: two joys may not be mixed together.
Each of the twenty-four books is a kallah, and Megillas Esther, once it became one of them, became a kallah; the joy of the Megillah is the joy of a kallah.
The joy of Purim is a joy with the Jewish people in all their situations, even the lowest, and that is its connection to the joy of a kallah.

catalogTitle: Asking Forgiveness ערב יו”כ - A Deeper Understanding

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yom Kippur, the fortieth day from Rosh Chodesh Elul, reaches the untouched innermost point of every Jew where all of Klal Yisrael is one, which is why appeasing one's fellow and receiving only thirty-nine lashes belong to Erev Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shulchan Aruch siman 606, which holds three halachos for Erev Yom Kippur yet is captioned only for appeasing one's fellow. He recalls Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz's one talk in the beis medrash about Yechida, the level where all souls merge as Knesses Yisrael, and the call to meet it on Yom Kippur. Through the Rambam on coerced consent and the Ohr HaChaim on Korach he shows that the point of Yaakov Avinu in every Jew stays unblemished. The Ramban ties forty lashes to the forty days of a fetus's formation; only thirty-nine are given because the first point is never damaged. He applies this to Adam's thirty-nine curses, the thirty-nine melachos and Yosef, who saw his father's image. Yom Kippur is the fortieth day of the year's formation, a day of unity and a mikveh, sealed at Ne'ilah.

en: Yechida, the highest level of the soul, is where all Jewish souls merge into the one soul of Knesses Yisrael, and on Yom Kippur a Jew can make contact with it.
Deep in every Jew's heart is a point drawn from Yaakov Avinu that wants only the will of Hashem and that no sin can blemish.
A transgression blemishes thirty-nine of the forty stages of a person's formation, but not the first point where Hashem began creating him, so the Torah gives only thirty-nine lashes.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation of the year, and Yom Kippur, the fortieth day, is where a Jew touches Yechida and the oneness of Knesses Yisrael.
Because Yom Kippur is a day of unity, one cannot enter it while in conflict with another Jew, which is why appeasing one's fellow belongs to Erev Yom Kippur.
Yom Kippur is itself a mikveh, filled through the teshuvah of the forty days, and its climax is the sealing of Ne'ilah.

title.en: Siman 606 and Rav Shraga Feivel's talk

summary.en: The Rav notes that Shulchan Aruch siman 606 contains three halachos, appeasing one's fellow, receiving lashes and a third, yet its caption names only appeasing, and asks why. He then recalls how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz once interrupted the learning to speak about Yechida and urged the bochurim to find the moment on Yom Kippur when they touch it and build their year on it.

title.en: The untouched point of Yaakov Avinu

summary.en: The Rav explains Yechida as the collective soul of Knesses Yisrael and brings the Rambam that coerced consent counts, because deep down every Jew wants Hashem's will. He traces this inner point to Yaakov Avinu, the trunk of the tree, and brings the Ohr HaChaim that Korach is not called a son of Yisrael because his blemish reached his fathers but not Yaakov.

title.en: Forty lashes and thirty-nine

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that lashes number forty because a sinner damages the forty days of his formation, and asks why only thirty-nine are given. He answers that the first point, where Hashem began creating the person, is never blemished: it is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the heart, the hidden love of the Tanya, untouched even in the worst Jew, and likewise Adam's sin brought thirty-nine curses but not a fortieth.

title.en: Yosef, the fortieth day and unity

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's count of thirty-nine or forty mentions of melachah, depending on Yosef's 'melachto', and explains that Yosef, near breaking, saw the image of Yaakov Avinu, the point that cannot be destroyed. He then counts forty days of formation from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the fortieth day when a Jew touches Yechida and Knesses Yisrael, and concludes that one must be reconciled with every Jew to enter it.

title.en: Why these halachos share one siman

summary.en: The Rav returns to siman 606: lashes are received on Erev Yom Kippur, the thirty-ninth day, and never forty, because the fortieth day is Yom Kippur where no sin reaches. Citing Rav Yaakov Emden that the Shulchan Aruch was written with ruach hakodesh, he explains why appeasing and the thirty-nine lashes belong together, and adds the immersion of Erev Yom Kippur, since Yom Kippur itself is a mikveh.

title.en: The mikveh of Yom Kippur and Ne'ilah

summary.en: The Rav describes the forty days of Elul as pouring forty se'ah of teshuvah into the mikveh of Yom Kippur, the day the pure point surfaces in every Jew. Like the Kohen Gadol, every Jew enters the Kodesh HaKodashim of his own heart, and at Ne'ilah each one re-enacts the tribes' declaration at Yaakov Avinu's bedside, a seal that remains all year. He closes with blessings for the coming year.

catalogTitle: כסף של אהבה' שקלים כנגד 'י' שבשם ד'

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the silver of the shekalim carries the power of love for Hashem, that Parshas Shekalim corresponds to the yud and the tip of the yud of Hashem's Name, the Jew's inner point that no sin and no Haman can reach, and he shows this through the haftarah of Yehoash.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Moshe's accounting of the Mishkan's silver and the Gemara that Hashem preceded Haman's shekalim with ours. Everything in the world has a spiritual root: silver is the measure of love, gold of awe, and Hashem knows how many 'units' of love lie in a half-shekel. Adar is the month of Yosef and of blessing, which multiplies a hundredfold; this answers Tosafos' question how a hundred kikar of shekalim outweighed Haman's ten thousand. Adar's task is to complete Hashem's Name broken by Amalek, and Shekalim corresponds to the yud and its tip, the Kodesh HaKodashim. The haftarah's King Yehoash, saved in the Kodesh HaKodashim yet later the killer of Zechariah there, belongs to Parshas Shekalim, and his rescue shows that the innermost point of a Jew cannot be touched by sin. This point is revealed on Purim, which the Rav calls greater than Yom Kippur.

en: Silver is the measure of love and gold the measure of awe; a half-shekel of silver holds a set measure of love for Hashem, and that, not the cold metal, is what Hashem asked the Jews to give.
Adar is the month of blessing and of Yosef, and blessing multiplies up to a hundredfold, which is why the hundred kikar the Jews gave became ten thousand and outweighed Haman's ten thousand kikar.
Amalek broke Hashem's Name, and the work of Adar, through the four parshiyos and the four mitzvos of Purim, is to make the Name whole again.
Parshas Shekalim corresponds to the yud of Hashem's Name and to its tip, the Kodesh HaKodashim, the source from which everything comes.
Every Jew has an inner point, his own Kodesh HaKodashim, that no sin can blemish and no mitzvah can add to, and Purim reveals it.
Yehoash's soul is rooted in Parshas Shekalim, and the Kodesh HaKodashim saved him even though he would later defile it, to show that nothing can blemish that place.
