Chanukah lights and the Beis HaMikdash

title.en: One hundred versus one hundred and one times

summary.en: The Rav opens with the passuk that in the days of Moshiach the difference between one who serves Hashem and one who does not will be seen, and brings the Gemara that reviewing 100 times is not yet service while 101 times is. He explains why the standard was 100 and why the extra time counts so much.

title.en: Chanukah's candles: adding every night

summary.en: The Rav says Chanukah gives a small taste of the days of Moshiach and brings the Gemara's dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on the number of candles. Beis Hillel's adding corresponds to 'do good', and the mehadrin who add each night live by the spirit of the oved Hashem who does more than the standard.

title.en: The masmid who stops growing

summary.en: The Rav describes a bochur who fights his yetzer hara and becomes a masmid learning eight hours a day, and asks whether he remains an oved Hashem once that is his routine; he answers that he does not, since serving means always striving for more. The same applies to sur mei'ra, such as extra care in kashrus, and he stresses that the time to work on this is now, before Moshiach comes.

title.en: Every day new: Chanukah as chinuch

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the mitzvos should be in one's eyes as new every day, illustrating with the excitement of a bar mitzvah boy's first tefillin. He connects this to the name Chanukah, chinuch, a new beginning, like the first day of the zman when a new Gemara is opened.

title.en: The home as a Mikdash, every Jew a kohen

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Beis HaMikdash, and the Ran that one may not use their light, so the home takes on a glow of the Mikdash. Since preparing the lamps in the Mikdash was done by a kohen, each Jew becomes a kohen; to the Chasam Sofer's reading of the name Chashmonaim he adds that Chanukah spells 'kohen' and eight.

title.en: Why Chanukah is a cherished mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Rambam calls only the Chanukah lights a very cherished mitzvah, and answers that what comes through struggle and pain becomes dear, as milah was to Avraham Avinu. Chanukah was won with mesiras nefesh, when a few Chashmonaim went to war against the Greek armies.

title.en: Ikvesa d'Meshicha: the Satan's last meal

summary.en: The Rav cites Rav Elchonon Wasserman's Ikvesa d'Meshicha and the Gemara at the end of Sotah on how hard keeping mitzvos will be before Moshiach. With a mashal of a condemned man's last meal he explains that the Satan, soon to be slaughtered, is now given unprecedented permission, which is why so many new inventions and temptations have appeared, to test who will be an oved Hashem.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh in small things

summary.en: The Rav explains that nefesh means one's will, so giving up a desire is mesiras nefesh, from giving one's life down to holding back. His examples are not looking at what one should not see, not making a hurtful joke in the lunchroom and not talking during seder; each is a tiny fraction of the Akeidah, and Chanukah is a time to check whether one serves by routine.

title.en: Chanukah remembers the barren

summary.en: The Rav closes with the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah is like Rosh Hashanah, the day the barren were remembered. He explains that one who is not fruitful in learning or in tefillah is also called barren, lists the seven barren women ending with Tziyon, and calls on his listeners to daven to be healed of barrenness in Torah and tefillah and for Tziyon's children to return.

catalogTitle: דרוש והתעוררות: חודש הכולל' יום שהוא למעלה מהשגתינו' מצוות היום

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the war against Amalek needs a power that includes all of Klal Yisrael, which Shaul in his humility sought through the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, and which Purim in Adar Sheni, the month that includes all months, brings down as a light beyond understanding.

abstract.en: Opening with the Chasam Sofer's call to explain Purim to the people, the Rav turns to the haftarah of Shaul and Amalek and asks why Shmuel first reminds Shaul that he was anointed king, and what Shaul meant by claiming he fulfilled Hashem's word and by answering that he kept the animals for sacrifices. He builds an answer from the order of the three mitzvos on entering the land: a king, who includes the whole nation, is needed to fight Amalek, who includes all impurity. Through Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh, the avos and the shevatim, and the stones of the choshen, he shows that Binyamin, whose stone lacks the names of the avos, holds the unity of the mizbeach. Shaul, too humble to see himself as king, sought that power through korbanos. Adar Sheni includes all months, so Haman's lottery failed. The Rav ends with the light revealed at the Megillah reading and the mitzvos of the day.

en: The war against Amalek, who includes all impurity, needs a king, who includes the whole nation; this is why appointing a king comes before wiping out Amalek and building the Beis HaMikdash.

Shabbos is the unity of the avos, while Rosh Chodesh and the twelve months correspond to the shevatim, the branches; the stones of the choshen belong to the shevatim, yet the names of the avos engraved on them bring in unity.
Binyamin's stone carries none of the letters of the avos, because Binyamin himself is the unity of Klal Yisrael: the mizbeach stands in his portion.
Shaul, out of humility, did not consider himself a true king, so he sought the all-including power through the mizbeach by taking the animals of Amalek for korbanos.

Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month, includes all the months, so the war against Haman took place in it, and Haman's lottery erred in seeing Adar only as Binyamin's month and the month of Moshe's passing.
At the reading of the Megillah a hidden and awesome world is revealed once a year, from which all salvations come.

Shaul and the war against Amalek
appointing a king before wiping out Amalek

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's call to explain Purim

summary.en: The Rav opens by saying Purim is a day nobody understands, and reads from the Chasam Sofer that the people celebrate without knowing what Purim is, so the sages used to gather them and explain it. He excuses his own speaking with the Chofetz Chaim's parable of the peasant who brought dirty water to put out a fire in the king's palace.

title.en: Shaul and Amalek in the haftarah

summary.en: The Rav reads the haftarah and asks why Shmuel prefaces the command to fight Amalek with 'Hashem sent me to anoint you king'. He retells how Shaul spared Agag and the animals and then told Shmuel he had fulfilled Hashem's word, and notes that from Agag's one night came Haman and the miracle of Purim.

title.en: Shaul's puzzling answers to Shmuel

summary.en: The Rav asks how Shaul could claim he fulfilled Hashem's word, and what kind of reply 'to bring korbanos' is to Shmuel's 'though you are small in your eyes, you are the head of the tribes of Israel'. He explains Shaul's later excuse, 'I feared the people', as referring to Doeg, who was considered equal to the whole nation.

title.en: Three mitzvos and the gift of the nesi'im

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that three mitzvos were commanded on entering the land, a king, wiping out Amalek and building the Beis HaMikdash, and asks why a king must come before Amalek. He then turns to the nesi'im who brought the shoham and milu'im stones, with Rashi's criticism that they waited to complete what was missing.

title.en: Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh, avos and shevatim

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Shabbos, fixed by Hashem and corresponding to the avos and to unity, with Rosh Chodesh and the twelve months, which correspond to the shevatim, the branches of the tree. The Mikdash and Yerushalayim are of the aspect of Shabbos, while the twelve stones of the choshen, each in its tribe's color, belong to the shevatim.

title.en: The choshen stones and Binyamin's mizbeach

summary.en: The Rav asks why the stones, which belong to the shevatim, are counted among the Mishkan's donations, and answers with the Gemara that 'Avraham Yitzchak Yaakov shivtei Yeshurun' was engraved on them, six letters to a stone. Binyamin's stone gets none of those letters, and the Rav explains that Binyamin needs none: the mizbeach, which unites all of Klal Yisrael, stands in his portion.

title.en: Moshe and Bilaam, the king and Amalek

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer on 'no prophet arose in Israel like Moshe': Moshe included all of Klal Yisrael, so he had to stand in tefillah during the war with Amalek, who includes all impurity and is bound up with Bilaam. From this he explains why a king, who includes the whole nation, must be appointed before the war on Amalek and the building of the Mikdash.

title.en: Shaul's humility and his korbanos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shaul, who hid among the vessels and saw himself as coming from Binyamin, the last tribe, did not believe he was truly king and lacked the all-including power. He therefore took the animals of Amalek as korbanos for the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, to draw that power from it; Shmuel's words 'you are the head of the tribes of Israel' answer him, and 'I feared the people' meant his regard for Doeg.

title.en: Adar Sheni, the all-including month

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month, includes all months, so the war against Haman happened in it. Haman's lottery saw Adar as Binyamin's month without the power of the avos and as the month Moshe died, but he did not know Mordechai was a spark of Moshe, and the Gemara reads the names of the advisors around Achashverosh as a list of korbanos, the power of Binyamin's mizbeach.

title.en: Purim as a renewed kabbalas haTorah

summary.en: Turning to Purim itself, the Rav says it is like Shavuos, a renewed acceptance of the Torah with love, with three days of preparation before it. Purim carries the power of Shabbos and more: the extra soul that comes for moments at the Kedushah of Shabbos is present the whole day of Purim, beginning with the Megillah.

title.en: The awesome world revealed at the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav reads from the sefer Yesod Yosef that a hidden, awesome world is revealed only once a year, at the reading of the Megillah, and explains with the Alter Rebbe's siddur that a goral is above reason, which links Purim to Yom Kippur. Because the Megillah comes from so high a place it has no Name of Hashem and will never be nullified; one who reads it as past history does not fulfill the mitzvah, for its salvations happen anew each year.

title.en: Mishloach manos, matanos and the seudah

summary.en: The Rav goes through the mitzvos of the day: in sending mishloach manos a Jew arouses Hashem to send him portions, tzedakah on Purim rises to a higher world, and the drinking must not disturb others. He reads the Kedushas Levi that the Purim seudah should be eaten with joy in accepting the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, and compares each bite to taking a vitamin that brings in that strength.

title.en: From Purim to Pesach; Mordechai at every seudah

summary.en: The Rav quotes the Stoliner Rebbe that as Purim goes, so goes Pesach, and the Chesed L'Avraham that the thirty days before Pesach, beginning with Purim, start Hashem's taking Jews out of impurity. He describes all the Purim seudos as one seudah of unity, tells of Mordechai HaTzaddik appearing at Reb Pinchas of Koretz's seudah, and closes that Purim is above comprehension and above all the festivals.

catalogTitle: המתיקות' הקדושה והאורות של "האגרת הזאת"

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah is a personal letter, an iggeres, sent to every Jew, spread open with lights that come down to even the lowest generation, so that Purim can bring great salvation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that the Gemara expounds the Megillah at length, as it does for no other Yom Tov, and that people celebrate Purim without knowing what it is. Through stories of R' Elazar of Amsterdam and the Slonimer Rebbe he shows that Purim, when Hashem comes down to us as Yom Kippur raises us up, is a day to bring salvation. Each tzaddik serves Purim by his own root, yet all roots meet in the Megillah. Its lights exceed even Shabbos, but they are hidden, and Hashem loves those who serve Him in hiddenness. The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter addressed to each Jew, and unlike other lofty mitzvos that are kept covered, it is spread open so its lights reach the world. After the Spinka story of a soul that found its tikkun through a Megillah read on Pesach, he teaches that each lower generation's Purim is greater, and calls for a battle of Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

en: On Yom Kippur a Jew must rise up to Hashem, while on Purim Hashem comes down to the Jews, even into the place of exile.
Each tzaddik and each Jew serves Hashem on Purim according to the root of his soul, but all the roots come together in the Megillah.
The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter, because it was written to every single Jew personally.
Lofty mitzvos such as the shofar, the challos and the matzos are kept covered, but the Megillah is spread out entirely, so that its lights spread through the world.
Since Purim's nature is to come down to the lowest levels, the Purim of a lower generation is greater than any before it.
Purim is a battle, and the Jews' weapons in it are Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

candidateTopics: Purim as a battle against Amalek

title.en: Why one must speak about Purim

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Gemara expounds the Megillah like a midrash, as it does for no other Yom Tov, and brings the Chasam Sofer that people celebrate Purim without knowing what it is. He tells how R' Elazar of Amsterdam brought salvation on Purim through drinking and dancing rather than Tehillim.

title.en: Purim brings salvation in exile

summary.en: The Rav explains that Purim joins miracle and nature, and is a weekday Yom Tov of exile; citing the Zohar, he says that on Purim Hashem comes down to the Jews as on Yom Kippur they rise to Him. He tells of the Slonimer Rebbe's extra Purim seudah for the sake of salvation, and says Purim must bring salvation now, when Jewish blood is being spilled.

title.en: Each tzaddik serves Purim by his root

summary.en: The Rav describes how differently tzaddikim conducted Purim, from Slonim to Komarna, and brings the Chasam Sofer on the separate gate of each tribe to show that every soul has its own root, yet all roots meet in the Megillah and in Mordechai. He tells how the Avnei Nezer's father merited his son by learning all Purim, and warns against jumping from one avodah to another.

title.en: The hidden lights of the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kedushas Levi and the Chasam Sofer that the light of Megillas Esther is greater than that of the Torah of Moshe, and explains that Purim's lights exceed even Shabbos but are clothed and hidden. Citing R' Yitzchak of Vorka, he calls the days the Megillah may be read early the three days of preparation before a kabbalas haTorah of love.

title.en: Keser malchus for a generation of hiddenness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem loves the generation of hiddenness, in which the sweetness of serving Him has been taken away, and contrasts it with earlier Chassidim, such as a Chabadnik who davened until four in the afternoon with tears. Whoever serves Him without that sweetness is like Esther and merits keser malchus; citing the Avodas Yisroel, he adds that Purim is like Shabbos.

title.en: The Megillah as a personal letter

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Megillah is called both a sefer and an iggeres: a sefer is written for whoever wants to buy it, while a letter is sealed and addressed to one person. Every Jew receives the Megillah from Mordechai and Esther as a private letter, like a yeshiva bochur reading his parents' news that his baby brother has grown an inch.

title.en: Covered mitzvos and the spread-out Megillah

summary.en: The Rav shows that mitzvos from a higher world are kept covered: the shofar, the Shabbos challos, the matzos (covered all Pesach in Chernobyl) and the Sefer Torah. The Megillah, though from a high world, is spread out entirely like a letter, and citing the Kozhnitzer Maggid he explains that this reveals the hidden and spreads its lights over all creation.

title.en: Moshiach, the wine of Purim and asking for all

summary.en: The Rav brings that Mordechai is a bechinah of Moshiach and the Megillah will be understood only when Moshiach comes, and that the Purim seudah resembles the feast of the future. The wine of Purim is a higher wine than that of Shabbos Kiddush, and since Hashem tells Esther 'what is your request', on Purim one may ask for everything; even a simple Jew can rise to a tzaddik's heichal.

title.en: The Spinka story: Purim on Pesach night

summary.en: The Rav tells the story the Imrei Yosef of Spinka told about 'a young man': reading the Megillah on the second night of Pesach, he was approached by a soul that had missed its Purim tikkun. The heavenly court asked him whether that night could be Purim, and he ruled that since Haman was hanged on Pesach, it could, and the soul received its tikkun.

title.en: The greatest Purim and the call to battle

summary.en: The Rav explains that as the world falls lower each year, Purim, which comes down to us, grows greater, and tells how Mordechai came to rejoice with a lonely tzaddik. Citing the Rosh, he compares Ta'anis Esther to Moshe's tefillah in the war with Amalek, and closes that Purim is a battle to be fought with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

catalogTitle: #1 A Beloved Mitzvah Because it was Acquired with Hardship

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvah of Chanukah is especially dear because Klal Yisrael acquired it with mesiras nefesh, and that its light carries kedushah into the darkness of night, the left side and the galus.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear, and notes that it is the last mitzvah the Chachamim instituted. He describes how the Greeks tried to impose their culture of strength and beauty and to uproot Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the mitzvos that show Klal Yisrael's chosenness, and how the Chashmonaim fought with mesiras nefesh. What is acquired through pain becomes dear, as with Avraham's milah and the Mishnah's cow, and so Chanukah is beloved. He compares the Hellenists to the Jewish Communists in Russia and the mesiras nefesh of today's returnees. He then explains the name Chashmonaim, the growing lights, and how Chanukah, lit at night, on the left and in the public domain at the tekufah of Teves, invades the realm of tumah, as Yosef's trial shows. Chanukah brings the Shechinah down to the lowest; he closes with the opportunity of this year, 5760.

en: The Rav explains the Rambam's statement that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear: something acquired through pain and mesiras nefesh becomes dear to the one who sacrificed for it.
The Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah because these three mitzvos show the chosenness and distinction of Klal Yisrael.
The Rav says the forces of kedushah and tumah are balanced so that there is free choice; night, the left side and the public domain belong to tumah, which is why most mitzvos are done by day.

Since the Greeks invaded the domain of kedushah, the Beis HaMikdash, Chanukah is lit at night, on the left side of the door, in the public domain, at the longest nights of Teves, carrying kedushah into the domain of tumah.
Unlike Shabbos, when a Jew rises toward the kedushah, on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down even below ten tefachim, so that even souls far removed can be kindled.
The Rav says the year 5760 holds a special chance for the geulah, with Chanukah beginning and ending on Shabbos, and one should use it to produce kedushah to offset the forces of the year 2000.

title.en: The Rambam: a very dear mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear, notes that the Rambam says this of no other mitzvah, and explains that Chanukah is the last mitzvah the Chachamim instituted, completing the letters of the Aseres HaDibros that make up a crown.

title.en: The Greek culture of strength and beauty

summary.en: The Rav describes how the Greeks sought to force their culture, the worship of beauty and strength, on the Jews, and contrasts it with the Jewish view, bringing the Gemara's story of the wise man and the queen's wine. He then says sports, which come from the Greeks, are nonsense whose heroes are often criminals.

title.en: Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and the mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Greeks targeted Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, which show Klal Yisrael's chosenness, and tells how the Chashmonaim fought with mesiras nefesh. Through Rashi on Avraham's milah and the Mishnah's cow that loves the calf it bore in pain, he concludes that Chanukah, acquired with suffering, is therefore the Rambam's 'very dear mitzvah'.

title.en: Hellenists then, Communists in Russia

summary.en: The Rav compares the Hellenist Jews who sided with the Greeks to the Jewish Communists in Russia, cites the Chofetz Chaim that a small army of mesiras nefesh would have won, and describes the return to Yiddishkeit today, including thirty teenage boys who underwent a bris in Russia.

title.en: The name Chashmonaim and the growing lights

summary.en: Building on the Midrash that Hashem answered Haman's envy of the Yamim Tovim with Purim, the Rav suggests that Chashmon stands for Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: the Greeks wanted to abolish three mitzvos and Hashem added a fourth. He explains that unlike every other mitzvah, Chanukah grows each night, a renewal tied to the word chinuch.

title.en: Kedushah and tumah: day and night, right and left

summary.en: The Rav says the Greeks invaded the Beis HaMikdash, so we invade their territory. He explains that kedushah and tumah are balanced to allow free choice, that night is the domain of tumah, as the passuk of the beasts roaming at night shows, and that therefore almost all time-bound mitzvos are by day, while kedushah is the right side and tumah the left.

title.en: Lit at night, on the left, in the public domain

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah is lit specifically at night, on the left side of the door and toward the public domain, which by the Zohar's explanation belongs to the nations, and on the longest nights of Teves. He explains the lunar and solar years and how the tekufah once fell on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, the time the nations make their holiday.

title.en: Nittel, the calendars and Adam's festival

summary.en: The Rav mentions the minhag not to learn on Nittel and explains the two dates it is kept, through the Julian and Gregorian calendars. He then brings the Gemara that Adam HaRishon, seeing the days shorten after his sin, feared the world was returning to darkness until the tekufah, when he made a festival that later generations turned into an idolatrous holiday.

title.en: Yosef's trial on the tekufah and the letters of Yavan

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yosef's trial with Potiphar's wife fell on a day of the nations' festival, explains that it was the tekufah, a day of no Torah learning, which made the trial greater, and reads 'kehayom' as the twenty-fifth day. Chanukah on the twenty-fifth offsets this by bringing kedushah into the long nights of Teves, growing each night, while the letters of Yavan show tumah spreading downward.

title.en: The Shechinah comes down to the lowest

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, yet the Chanukah lights are placed below ten. Oils and wicks unfit for Shabbos are allowed on Chanukah, because on Shabbos a Jew rises up while on Chanukah the kedushah comes down; since the soul is a lamp, even those whom Shabbos does not reach can be kindled on Chanukah.

title.en: Two Shabbosos of Chanukah in 5760

summary.en: The Rav notes that this year Chanukah begins and ends on Shabbos, in a year he describes as having a great chance for Moshiach, which the nations mimic with the year 2000 and heavy missionary spending. He urges producing kedushah through learning, mitzvos and the Chanukah lights, and closes with the gematria of eight lights as 2000, offsetting the tumah of that year.

catalogTitle: גודל כח היום; הדרכה איך לנהוג בו

oneLiner.en: The Rav describes the great power of Purim, a day of turning around and of accepting the Torah with love whose holiness lasts all day, and guides how to keep it: with joy, with kavanah in its foods, without drunkenness, and with tefillah for every yeshuah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Megillah's twice-mentioned 'turning over' and says Adar is a time when a person can turn himself around, daven for Klal Yisrael, and draw on the strong mazal of Adar. He explains that the days before Purim are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos, because on Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah willingly, and brings the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's holiness exceeds even the Torah of Moshe. The kedushah of Keser stays all Purim day, and Purim is greater than Yom Kippur, so it must be met with joy. He then teaches that holy foods become part of a person, warns sharply against drunkenness, explains why the Megillah is opened entirely, and answers why tzaddikim did not ask for the redemption on Purim. A story of the Shomer Emunim shows Purim's power for yeshuos.

en: Adar is a month of 'turning over', when a person can turn himself around: daven, learn and fix his middos.
On Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah with love, so the days before it are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos.
The kedushah of Keser, present on Shabbos only during Kedushah of Musaf, remains the whole day of Purim, and no accuser has a hold then.
The foods of Shabbos and Yom Tov carry the holiness of the day and become part of the person who eats them with kavanah.
Drinking on Purim should be a glass of wine and a short nap; getting drunk is a disgrace and causes chillul Hashem.
Everything one needs can be drawn from the Megillah, and on Purim tzaddikim have permission to bring yeshuos they cannot bring all year.

title.en: Adar, the month of turning over

summary.en: The Rav notes that the Megillah speaks of 'turning over' twice, for the day and for the month, and says a person can use Adar to turn himself around. He adds that tefillos are accepted from Adar to Sivan, urges davening for Klal Yisrael in its danger, and brings the Gemara that a Jew's mazal is strong in Adar.

title.en: Three days of preparation before Purim

summary.en: The Rav goes through the Mishnah's days for reading the Megillah and the walled cities, then explains that the three days before Purim are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, because on Purim the Jews accepted the Oral Torah willingly and with love.

title.en: The kedushah of Keser all Purim day

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah is holier than the Torah of Moshe, the Rav explains that the kedushah of Keser stays all Purim day, that Purim is greater than Yom Kippur, and that Purim must therefore be met with great joy, not with tension.

title.en: Purim is not a holiday of wildness; holy foods

summary.en: The Rav rejects the view of Purim as a Jewish version of the gentiles' wild holiday, and through a parable of an egg that 'needs mazal' to end up in a Jewish Shabbos dish, he describes the fixed Shabbos foods and the special Purim foods as holding great secrets, to be eaten with kavanah.

title.en: What one eats becomes part of him

summary.en: The Rav explains that unlike other mitzvos, food becomes part of the person; this is why forbidden foods are so grave, and why each Yom Tov has its food: matzah on Pesach, dairy on Shavuos, eating in the sukkah, holishkes on Simchas Torah, latkes on Chanukah and hamantaschen on Purim.

title.en: The Purim seudah and the danger of drunkenness

summary.en: The Rav says the seudah and wine are an obligation, but getting drunk is not for this generation: most tzaddikim drank a glass of wine, the Satmar Rav was an exception whose drunkenness revealed hidden Torah, and the poskim say to drink a little and nap. He describes the disgrace and chillul Hashem of drunkenness, from Adam and Noach to today's emergency rooms.

title.en: The open Megillah and its yeshuos

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Sefer Torah, kept covered, with the Megillah, opened entirely before reading so its holiness spreads to the whole world, and shows that every kind of yeshuah is found in the Megillah. He adds that Purim is like Shabbos, so one wears Shabbos clothes, and that at the seudah all yeshuos can be drawn.

title.en: Why tzaddikim did not ask for the geulah; the ke'arah

summary.en: Reading 'what is your request' as Hashem asking Klal Yisrael on Purim, the Rav asks why great tzaddikim did not ask for the geulah, and answers that they were shown the purpose of galus. He tells how the Shomer Emunim on Purim promised children for a silver ke'arah, says every Jew can enter the Holy of Holies on Purim, and closes with practical words for the day.

catalogTitle: ביטול קליפת עמלק של "רפו ידיהם מן התורה"

oneLiner.en: Before Purim, the Rav explains that Torah learned with love sweetens harsh decrees, that Amalek's power is the slackening and cooling toward Torah, and calls on his community to strengthen fixed learning, davening together and daily mussar.

abstract.en: Following the Chasam Sofer's custom of speaking before Purim, the Rav compares Adar, especially the second Adar, to Elul as a month of teshuvah. He asks why Rashi on the verse 'what did they see… and what came upon them' departs from the Gemara's reading. Bringing the Ohr HaChaim, he explains that Torah learned with love and awe rises to Binah and sweetens judgments, which otherwise are sweetened by the passing of tzaddikim, as with Avishai ben Tzeruyah. Following the Chasam Sofer, Mordechai and Esther meant to give their lives as an atonement; the result was 'kiymu v'kiblu', Torah with love, which made that unnecessary. Amalek attacked at Refidim, when hands slackened from Torah, and he cools a person off. The Rav proposes an hour of learning before Maariv, brings the Yismach Yisrael's takanos on learning and davening together, warns about assimilation, tells two stories, and urges daily mussar.

en: Adar, the last month counted from Nissan, is a month of teshuvah like Elul, and the second Adar of a leap year even more so.
Torah learned with love and awe of Hashem rises to Binah, the root of all judgments, and sweetens them there.
Mordechai's and Esther's self-sacrifice brought about 'kiymu v'kiblu', the Jews' acceptance of the Torah with love, which is the answer to 'what came upon them'.
Amalek's strength comes from 'Refidim', the slackening of hands from Torah, and his effect is to cool a person off.
The Rav proposes that whoever can should come to the beis medrash and learn for an hour before Maariv, as a commitment without a vow.
Following the Yismach Yisrael, the souls of a chevra are bound together above, so learning and davening together gives strength and more kavanah.
The Rav urges everyone to take on learning a mussar sefer every day, as the Chasam Sofer had his students learn Chovos HaLevavos before the shiur.

Adar as a month of teshuvah
learning and davening together as a chevra

title.en: Preparing for Purim; Adar as a month of teshuvah

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer's custom of speaking before Purim, the Rav explains that Purim is a renewed acceptance of the Torah and needs preparation. He brings Rav Shalom of Belz that Adar, like Elul, is a time of teshuvah, especially the second Adar, and asks for mercy for the tzaddikim and all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: What did they see, and what came upon them

summary.en: The Rav reads the verse 'what did they see… and what came upon them' and the Gemara's explanation of it for Achashverosh, Haman, Mordechai and Esther. He asks why Rashi follows a different version, which leaves the last question unanswered, when the Gemara seems closer to the plain meaning.

title.en: Torah with love sweetens judgments

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that Torah learned with love and awe rises to Binah, the root of judgments, and sweetens them; without such Torah, judgments are sweetened through the passing of tzaddikim. He brings the Gemara about the plague in King David's time that ended with the death of Avishai ben Tzeruyah.

title.en: Mordechai and Esther as an atonement; kiymu v'kiblu

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that Mordechai refused to bow and Esther invited Haman so that their deaths would atone for the generation. The result was 'kiymu v'kiblu', Torah accepted with love, which can sweeten judgments without the tzaddikim's sacrifice, and this is why Rashi chooses this reading as the plain meaning.

title.en: Not letting go; Amalek and slackened hands

summary.en: From the Chasam Sofer the Rav learns that Mordechai kept praying and fasting after the first sign of salvation, since improvement can weaken prayer while the decree still stands. He then explains Amalek's attack at Refidim as coming from the slackening of hands from Torah, and Haman, Amalek's descendant, as rising when the Jews were lax in mitzvos.

title.en: An hour of learning before Maariv

summary.en: Since the month of Adar calls for strengthening in Torah, the Rav notes that the evening learning his community once had has lapsed, and proposes, without a vow, that whoever can should learn in the beis medrash for an hour before Maariv. He stresses that this is meant to strengthen diligence and the sense of responsibility, so that it becomes second nature.

title.en: The Yismach Yisrael's takanos for the beis hachasidim

summary.en: The Rav reads the Yismach Yisrael of Alexander's takanos: to learn in the beis hachasidim, since souls that stood together at Sinai come together in one chevra, and to daven there with a minyan, waiting patiently rather than being exacting. He adds the takanah against idle talk in the beis hachasidim and the measured speech of Shabbos.

title.en: A fateful time: assimilation and redemption

summary.en: The Rav describes the present as a fateful time, pointing to the mass intermarriage of Jews, which he calls a destruction greater than the Holocaust about which people are silent. He compares it to Ezra's time before the Second Temple, applies Mordechai's words to Esther, 'if you are silent at this time', and says we can be Hashem's instruments for the salvation by strengthening one another.

title.en: 'Asher karcha': Amalek cools us off

summary.en: On 'asher karcha baderech' the Rav says Amalek cooled them off, and asks why the fiery davening of the chevra's early years has cooled, calling for a cheshbon hanefesh. He tells a story he heard from the Satmar Rav of a tzaddik who once skipped his custom of mayim emtza'im, traced it to a conversation with a Sabbatean, and was troubled that he had become worse.

title.en: Az nidberu: the value of the chevra

summary.en: The Rav says learning together at night increases friendship, and brings Malachi's last prophecy, 'then those who fear Hashem spoke to one another', for a dark time before Moshiach. He tells a story of a chassan at the Stoliner Rebbe's court who left the Rebbe's minyan, and lists the treasured parts of his own community's davening.

title.en: Yekar: feeling the preciousness; daily mussar

summary.en: Bringing the Sfas Emes on 'v'yekar', the Rav says avodah was precious to the Jews then and must be precious now, not given away for money, and calls for a cheshbon hanefesh in Adar. Following the Chasam Sofer, he urges learning a mussar sefer daily, and closes with a tefillah for salvation and redemption.

catalogTitle: שמחים בפורים שלכל עומק שנופל יהודי' מכל מקום הוא חלק מה' (שייכות לפרשת זכור ותצוה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim is the Yom Tov of the 'stragglers', the Jews who fell furthest, because however low a Jew falls he remains Hashem's portion, and on Purim he should rejoice in that.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Parshas Tetzaveh, read in the week of Zachor, where Moshe Rabbeinu's name is missing. Haman chose Adar thinking Moshe's merit had ended, but for Jews there is no 'death of Moshe': a Yehoshua always carries the Torah onward. Amalek attacked the stragglers whom the cloud had cast out of the camp, Jews the Torah calls 'not fearing G-d', and yet Hashem wages war for them. The darkness is strongest just before dawn, as in Mitzrayim, Bavel and before Moshiach. Purim came by lot, without effort, showing that every Jew is Hashem's portion; a king's child who falls into filth remains his child. The Megillah is an iggeres, a personal letter to each Jew, the more so the further he is. After stories and the Purim tefillos, the Rav warns against mockery and ends with Aharon, who earned the choshen by rejoicing in his brother's greatness.

en: For the Jewish people there is no 'death of Moshe': after Moshe always comes a Yehoshua who carries the Torah further.
Even a Jew who was cast out of the camp and seems not to fear Hashem remains so dear to Him that Hashem wages war on Amalek for his sake.
The darkness is strongest at the end of every exile, just before dawn, and so it is in the time before Moshiach.
Purim came by lot, without effort, which shows what is truly one's own: every Jew is Hashem's portion, and no sin can make Him abandon His child.
Purim is the Yom Tov of the stragglers, and on it a Jew should rejoice in his point of Yiddishkeit, knowing he is a child of Hashem however far he fell.
Purim is a holy day of love and unity, not a time for mockery or for shaming another Jew.

joy in one's point of Yiddishkeit

title.en: Parshas Tetzaveh without Moshe's name

summary.en: The Rav notes that Parshas Tetzaveh, read in the week of Parshas Zachor, is the parsha in which Moshe Rabbeinu's name is not mentioned. He explains that 'zachor', remembering, applies to something that tends to be forgotten.

title.en: Achashverosh's feast and the Jew's hope

summary.en: The Rav describes the end of the seventy years of the Babylonian exile, when many thought the redemption would not come and Achashverosh celebrated his calculation. He explains, with the Zohar on Vayeshev, that the nations' hatred comes from the Jew's hope, and that kings will give the Jews anything except Yerushalayim.

title.en: No 'death of Moshe' for the Jews

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman chose Adar, the month of Moshe's passing, thinking his merit had ended, but for Jews there is no death of Moshe: a Yehoshua always comes after him to carry the Torah. He ties Zachor to the danger of forgetting Torah, brings the Gemara on reviewing a hundred and one times, and notes that Parshas Zachor itself mentions Yehoshua.

title.en: The outer Jews and Yaakov's gift to Esav

summary.en: The Rav speaks of very simple Jews who stand as if outside the Mishkan, and says Hashem will not give up any Jew. He brings the Midrash that the animals Yaakov sent to Esav were Jewish souls, which Moshiach will reclaim, and says that even souls caught by the nachash remain bound to Moshe Rabbeinu.

title.en: Amalek and those cast out of the camp

summary.en: The Rav explains that Amalek attacked Hashem's honor, yet Hashem forgoes His own honor, as the Gemara about Yeravam shows. Amalek struck the stragglers whom the cloud had cast out of the camp, whom the passuk calls 'not fearing G-d', and still Hashem declares war on Amalek for their sake.

title.en: The darkest hour before dawn

summary.en: The Rav says that even a Jew whom Avraham Avinu does not recognize as his child is important enough to Hashem to fight for. He explains that Adar ends the year, cloaked in nature, and that darkness grows strongest at the end of each exile: in Mitzrayim, in Bavel, and before Moshiach. Esther called out from this darkness, and Hashem did not give up even on the Jews who enjoyed Achashverosh's feast.

title.en: Purim by lot: the Jew as Hashem's portion

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the other Yamim Tovim, which need preparation, with Purim, which came by lot. A lot shows what is truly one's own without effort, and Jews are Hashem's portion. He explains that Yom Kippur is 'like Purim', that no sin can make Hashem reject a Jew, and that a king's child who falls into filth remains his child.

title.en: Purim belongs to the fallen Jew

summary.en: The Rav says the great joy of Purim is to know that one is a child of Hashem however far one has fallen, and that one who learned and davened well all year has, as it were, no special share in Purim, the day of the stragglers. Hashem tells the yetzer hara it has no right to touch a Jewish soul. He connects this to Esther's cry of Ayeles Hashachar and to matanos l'evyonim, Hashem's gifts to the poor.

title.en: The rose and Shoshanas Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav explains that colors hint at middos, red being din and distance. A rose is red, yet even from afar its scent is sweet, and Jews remain distinguished even when far. He describes the joy of Shoshanas Yaakov, of belonging to the people that accepts malchus Shamayim, and says Purim reveals Hashem's 'rav chesed', whose color is white.

title.en: The Megillah as a sefer and an iggeres

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Megillah is called both a sefer and an iggeres, and explains the difference: a book is for whoever wants it, while a letter is addressed to one person. A Jew may feel a sefer Torah is not for him, but no one refuses a letter from the king with his own name on it; the Megillah is such a letter to every Jew, the more so the further he is.

title.en: Purim's letters to every Jew and the avodah of Purim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim that on Purim one can ask for everything, but one needs sense, and tells of a man whose blessings were all fulfilled until Heaven made him a drunkard. Purim is made for the drunk and the stragglers; the King sends His letters to every province. He explains that the preparation for Pesach begins on Purim, and that the avodah of Purim is not a day of mikveh and Tehillim but rejoicing as a fallen Jew in one's point of Yiddishkeit.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam and the broken dam

summary.en: The Rav tells the story brought in seforim of Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam: when a dam broke on Purim, the queen sent for his tefillah, and he responded by drinking, dancing and rejoicing, and the danger passed. He explains that the Jews' will counts in Heaven because they do Hashem's will, and on Purim Hashem's will is feasting and joy.

title.en: Taanis Esther's tefillah and the light revealed on Purim

summary.en: The Rav says one must come before the King like Esther, and that on Taanis Esther one should find time to say the kapitel of Ayeles Hashachar. He reads from a sefer of one of the early mekubalim that a hidden world created in the days of Mordechai and Esther is revealed with the reading of the Megillah, a light of 'rav chesed' that Shabbos reveals only for a moment. Because this holiness is so great, he explains, it can only be received through drinking.

title.en: Not a day for mockery; Yom Kippur and Purim

summary.en: The Rav warns that Purim is a holy day of forgiveness and unity, not a time for foolishness, mockery or insulting others and the honor of Torah, which the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah never intended. He reads the end of Parshas Tetzaveh, where 'once a year' appears twice, as hinting at two atonements: the avodah of Yom Kippur and the 'avodah without avodah' of Purim, a Yom Tov for the stragglers.

title.en: Aharon's choshen: joy in another's greatness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Aharon merited the choshen on his heart because he rejoiced in the greatness of his younger brother Moshe. Purim is a time of love, without envy or shaming, when each Jew rejoices in his own point. A leader of Klal Yisrael, like Moshe who went from the mountain straight to the people and Aharon who carried their judgment on his heart, must not have himself in mind. He closes with a vort of Rabbi Mordechai of Lechovitch on joy that makes the soul shine.

catalogTitle: #2 Lighting the Candle of השם

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the empty receptacles of the Chanukah menorah stand for Jewish souls still waiting to be kindled, which will all be lit when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why the menorah has eight receptacles, most of them empty in the first nights, when a brachah should rest on fullness, as with a full cup for Kiddush and clearing empty dishes before bentching. To answer, he explains that Chanukah, unlike other Yamim Tovim, is by its very character a weekday. He then speaks of neshamos: the Satan snatches the finer souls away from their roots, and before Moshiach many return through teshuvah, as in the time of the Chashmona'im, who fought the Hellenized Jews and brought them back. Chanukah is a taste of Moshiach, which is why it has eight lights, eight being the number of Moshiach. Its candles belong in the reshus harabim, the Satan's territory, because a candle is a neshamah; each night another captive soul is kindled, and the empty receptacles are souls still waiting, until all are lit when Moshiach comes.

en: A brachah rests on fullness, so the Rav asks why the brachah on the Chanukah lights is said over a menorah with empty receptacles.
Chanukah is a weekday not because it is inferior, but because that is its very character.
The Satan snatches the finer neshamos, and those who return in teshuvah are often more devoted than those raised in Yiddishkeit.
Chanukah is a sampling of Moshiach, and its eight lights reflect that eight stands for Moshiach.
A candle is a neshamah; the Chanukah lights are kindled in the reshus harabim to rescue souls held captive in the Satan's territory.
The empty receptacles are souls still waiting to be lit; on the 'eighth night', when Moshiach comes, all will be kindled.

title.en: Why light over empty receptacles?

summary.en: The Rav opens on Kislev, the month of light, and asks why the menorah has eight receptacles that stand empty, when the Shechinah dwells in fullness and a brachah is said over a full cup and a cleared table. He adds that a mitzvah's depth is beyond us, but he will offer some insight into Chanukah.

title.en: A weekday Yom Tov and snatched neshamos

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Yamim Tovim, with special clothing and no work, with Chanukah, which is by its character a weekday. He then explains that the Satan snatches the finer neshamos in galus, that Moshiach will force him to return them, and that the present teshuvah movement already shows those who return to be especially devoted.

title.en: The Chashmona'im and eight as Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav describes the Hellenistic movement that drew away great souls, and the Chashmona'im's war against the Hellenized Jews, who were defeated and did teshuvah. Chanukah is therefore a taste of Moshiach, and he brings the Gemara that the Beis HaMikdash harp of seven strings will have eight in the days of Moshiach, so the menorah has eight lights.

title.en: Kindling captive souls in the reshus harabim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the reshus harabim is foreign territory, yet the Chanukah lights were meant to be lit there to bring kedushah into it. A candle is a neshamah, so each light rescues a captive soul; the empty receptacles are souls still begging to be lit, until all are kindled when Moshiach comes. He closes with the prayer for a new light in the brachah of Yotzer.

catalogTitle: נתגלה עולם חדש של “יחידה”

oneLiner.en: Reading from the Yesod Yosef, the Rav explains that the miracle of Purim created a new, awesome world above, the root of Mordechai's soul and the world of yechidah where all Jewish souls become one, and that on Purim this light comes down to this world for those who are united with all Jews.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with practical words for those traveling to Yerushalayim for Purim Meshulash: rest before the reading, hear the Megillah together with the public, and if a word is missed say it at once and catch up. He stresses that Purim is a serious, holy day and introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef with a story of the Beis Aharon. The Yesod Yosef says the miracle of Mordechai and Esther created a new holy world above, the root of Mordechai's soul, which is not revealed outward. The Rav ties it to Yom Kippur, called 'like Purim': both reach the world of yechidah, where all souls become one, and only through unity. On Yom Kippur we rise to it; on Purim it comes down. He discusses drinking on Purim, the special wine and tzedakah of the day, the blessing on the Megillah as a call to its light, the fully opened Megillah, and the ever-growing joy of Adar.

en: According to the Yesod Yosef, the miracle of Mordechai and Esther created a new, holy and awesome world above that had never existed before, and it is not revealed outward.
That world is the root of Mordechai's soul and is the world of yechidah, the level at which all Jewish souls merge into one soul.
Yom Kippur reaches the same world, but on Yom Kippur Jews rise up to it like angels, while on Purim the light comes down into this world, sanctifying even the body.
Just as one has no Yom Kippur without unity and forgiving one another, one cannot receive the light of Purim without achdus with all Jews.
The blessing 'al mikra Megillah' means calling the Megillah, calling its hidden light down, so it should be said and heard with trembling and with the intent to become a vessel for that light.
'When Adar enters, joy increases' means that joy must keep growing day by day through the month, just as from Rosh Chodesh Av the sadness keeps deepening until Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Preparing for Purim in Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav mentions his trip to Yerushalayim for Purim Meshulash and the jet lag he once felt at the Megillah reading. He advises travelers to rest beforehand, to hear the Megillah together with the public, and explains what to do if a word is missed.

title.en: Purim as a holy day; the Yesod Yosef

summary.en: Citing the Chasam Sofer on speaking about Purim beforehand, the Rav stresses that Purim is a serious, holy day, greater than Yom Kippur. He introduces the sefer Yesod Yosef and tells how the Beis Aharon praised a simple Jew who loved the words of Shir HaShirim without understanding them.

title.en: A new world: the root of Mordechai's soul

summary.en: The Rav reads the Yesod Yosef: Purim brought a new holy world into being, the root of Mordechai's soul, which is not revealed outward. He links it to Yom Kippur, 'like Purim', and explains that both are the world of yechidah, reached only through unity: on Yom Kippur we rise to it, on Purim it comes down.

title.en: How to drink on Purim

summary.en: The Rav sharply criticizes disgraceful drunkenness on Purim and contrasts it with the Satmar Rav, who drank and revealed secrets of the Torah. He describes how the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov drank a little and napped, and how Rabbi Avraham of Ciechanow drank a measured revi'is of wine.

title.en: The wine and tzedakah of Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the wine and the matanos l'evyonim of Purim are of a different kind, as an esrog becomes precious on Sukkos. He returns to the difference between Yom Kippur and Purim, saying the light comes down to this world on Purim, that one must pray for it, and that it requires achdus.

title.en: Unity against Haman, and calling the Megillah

summary.en: Against Haman's 'scattered and divided' and Amalek at Refidim, Purim is unity, expressed in mishloach manos joining all tables into one. The Rav says one must pray to merit the light, cites the Arizal, and explains that 'al mikra Megillah' means calling the hidden light of the Megillah down to us.

title.en: Kavanah at the blessing; the open Megillah

summary.en: Continuing the Yesod Yosef, the Rav explains that the one reading should say the blessing with trembling and that each listener should intend to become a vessel for the light now revealed. He then explains why the Megillah is opened fully and folded like a letter rather than rolled like a Sefer Torah: the hidden is revealed.

title.en: Joy that keeps growing in Adar

summary.en: The Rav recommends a kuntres of sources on Purim and answers a question he was asked at a sheva brachos: 'when Adar enters, joy increases' means joy grows greater every day, just as the mourning of Av deepens step by step until Tisha B'Av. He closes with a blessing for a joyous month and a bright Purim.

catalogTitle: יו"ט שמלמד איך לשחוק על העולם

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Purim, the day of Adar when miracles are cloaked in nature and Hashem's name is hidden, teaches a Jew to read the Megillah, history and his own life until he sees that Hashem pulls every string, and to laugh at the world's puppet show.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer: Purim is not a day of foolishness but a day whose light exceeds even the Torah of Moshe, and the Rabbonim used to speak before it to awaken teshuvah. He contrasts Nissan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, whose name comes from aderes, a cloak: the Purim miracles are wrapped in nature, and the Megillah never mentions Hashem's name. The Bnei Yissaschar's parable of the sick man and the 'coincidences' of the Megillah show that a hidden miracle is greater than the splitting of the sea. The concealment is Amalek's work, the klipah of chance and doubt; yet 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem, and His name hides in its initials. With the parable of a puppet show, the Rashash's watch and a doctor reading an X-ray, the Rav teaches that a Jew must learn to read the Megillah, the newspaper and his own day this way. He closes with the Yesod Yosef on the great light revealed at the Megillah reading, and asks that Purim be prepared for and kept seriously.

en: Purim is a very great day; the Chasam Sofer and the Kedushas Levi say the light of the Megillah is even greater than that of the Torah of Moshe.
Nissan is the month of open miracles that change nature; Adar, from aderes (a cloak), is the month of miracles wrapped in nature, and so the Megillah never mentions Hashem's name.
The concealment of Hashem is the klipah of Amalek, which makes a Jew say everything 'just happened' and casts doubt into his heart.
The whole world is Hashem's puppet show: kings and presidents only move because He pulls the strings, and one who knows this can look at the world and laugh.
Hashem's name is in fact everywhere in the Megillah, hidden in initials and between the words, and a Jew must learn to read the Megillah the way a doctor learns to read an X-ray.
The lesson of Purim is to see Hashem guiding history, current events and everything that happens to a person from Modeh Ani until he goes to sleep, and to carry this through the whole year.
At the Megillah reading a great light from a 'new world' is revealed, and a Jew must prepare himself through teshuvah to be a vessel to receive it.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: Purim is a great day

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that people mistake Purim for a day of foolishness, while the light of the Megillah is greater than that of the Torah of Moshe, as the Kedushas Levi also says. Therefore the Rabbonim used to speak before Purim to stir the people to teshuvah.

title.en: From Nissan to Adar: miracles seen and unseen

summary.en: The Rav explains that the months descend from Nissan, the month of open miracles, to Adar, the lowest. A nes is a banner raised for all to see, but a plain reading of the Megillah shows only a palace story without a single miracle or mention of Hashem; only a believing Jew sees the miracles there.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar's parable of the sick man

summary.en: The Rav tells the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man whose only cure and only doctor are across the sea, and both arrive by ship that very day. He applies it to the chain of 'just then' events in the Megillah and concludes that a miracle within nature is no smaller than the splitting of the sea, and even greater.

title.en: Adar as aderes, and the Adar of history

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adar comes from aderes, a cloak: its miracles are veiled in nature. Our generation, at the heels of Moshiach, lives in the Adar of history, with hidden miracles like the fall of Russia and the threat from Iraq; the Megillah too came at the end of the Babylonian exile. He brings the Midrash that 'the King' in the Megillah means Hashem.

title.en: Amalek covers Hashem's name

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem's name is missing if 'the King' means Him, and answers that the klipah of Amalek covers it: the Name and the Throne are incomplete while Amalek exists, Amalek 'happened upon you' and calls everything chance, and Amalek equals safek, doubt. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that hamelech, kes and Haman all equal 95.

title.en: The puppet show: laughing at the world

summary.en: The Rav describes a puppet show whose wooden figures dance only because experts above pull thin strings, and applies it to world leaders such as Bush and Saddam Hussein: Hashem moves them all. One who knows this can sit back, look at the world and laugh. The plain meaning of 'the King' is Achashverosh, the derash is Hashem, and the two do not contradict.

title.en: Hashem's name hidden between the words

summary.en: The Rav shows that Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah, as in the initials of 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom', which a chassidish ba'al koreh reads in one breath. Hashem watches through the cracks, as in 'mashgiach min hachalonos', and the Megillah reflects hester panim; one must learn to read it and to see Hashem's hand in every timely event.

title.en: The Rashash and the soldier's watch

summary.en: The Rav tells how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter visited the Rashash in Vilna when the Rashash's watch had broken; the Rashash trusted that Hashem would send him one, and a Jewish soldier arrived with a gold watch a dying comrade had asked him to give to a talmid chacham. The Rav calls it hashgachah pratis and says the more a Jew trusts, the more he sees it.

title.en: Reading the Megillah like an X-ray

summary.en: The Rav compares the Megillah to an X-ray: a layman sees only black and white, while a trained doctor reads it. No book of Tanach has as many commentaries, and every verse is a gear in the clock that brings the miracle. Reading it this way one can say the brachah She'asah Nissim, and learn to see Hashem in the newspaper, in history and in each day of one's life.

title.en: The Jewish people a miracle; Adar and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kuzari that the survival of the Jewish people through every exile and every Haman shows Hashem plainly. He then speaks of the holiness of Purim and Adar, Adar Sheni in particular, of Purim's link to Yom Kippur through the goral, of Hashem preparing the cure at the very moment of the sin, and of the Rebbe of Belz on doing teshuvah in Adar.

title.en: Hashem comes down on Purim; Purim salvations

summary.en: The Rav explains that the greatness of the Megillah is that holiness enters nature: on Yom Kippur we rise to Hashem, on Purim Hashem comes down to our lowest levels. Purim is a day of salvation for which one prepares with the teshuvah of Taanis Esther, and he recalls Stalin's end on Purim and the Scud missiles of the Gulf War, which ended on Purim.

title.en: The Megillah happens every year

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled the mitzvah, read as reading it as an old story: the Megillah happens every year. He describes Achashverosh, who hated Jews and the Beis Hamikdash and made his feast over a miscalculation of the seventy years, yet was forced to do good for the Jews; tzaddikim know how to read the Megillah and draw down such salvations.

title.en: The brachos of the Megillah; Esther's psalm

summary.en: The Rav explains the brachah 'al mikra megillah' through the Kozhnitzer Maggid: Megillas Esther means revealing what is hidden. The brachah after the Megillah is a combined brachah because all salvations are contained in it. He brings the Yesod Yosef that saying Tehillim 22, which Esther said, with kavanah on Taanis Esther is a segulah for salvation, and describes the great holiness at the Megillah reading.

title.en: The main Purim is by day

summary.en: The Rav explains that the main Megillah reading and the mitzvos of Purim are by day, and criticizes those who carouse all night, sleep through davening and doze through the Megillah. He says one should rise with a clear head, give matanos la'evyonim and mishloach manos, daven with kavanah and hear every word of the Megillah, serving with joy and closeness to Hashem.

title.en: Yesod Yosef: the new world revealed at the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav reads from the Yesod Yosef, praised in a haskamah of Rabbi Aharon of Chernobyl: the light of Purim, like the light of Kedushah on Shabbos, comes from a 'new world' that descends once a year at the Megillah reading. The brachah 'al mikra megillah' calls it down, to be said with awe, and each Jew must prepare to be a vessel; he closes that Purim is no joke but a day of great salvation.

catalogTitle: צריכים לחפש הקב"ה שהטמין עצמו בהמגילה ובעולם הטבע

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Hashem hid Himself in the Megillah and in the world of nature, His Name concealed in the first and last letters of its words, and that a Jew must search for Him until he finds Him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with this year's special Purim, when Yerushalayim has three days of Purim. On Purim, he says, holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written openly in the Megillah; the Midrash reads 'the King' as Hashem, and the miracles are clothed in nature. He then explains how the Name is hidden in the first or last letters of words: in order it signals the attribute of kindness, reversed it signals judgment. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the permutation of each month, and shows the Name in several verses of the Megillah, matching the Gemara's two blessings after the reading. With the story of Reb Baruch'l and the hidden child, he says Hashem hides and waits to be sought, and that the world, like the Megillah, is full of hidden miracles. He closes with the Maharal on the fifteenth of Adar, the full moon, and Shushan Purim falling on Shabbos, when the Megillah 'reads itself'.

en: On Purim holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written openly in the Megillah; He is hidden in the word 'the King' and in miracles clothed in nature.
The Name hidden in the initial letters of words in order expresses kindness; reversed, or in the final letters, it expresses judgment.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, each month has its own permutation of the Name, and the month's character matches it, as with Nissan and Tammuz.
Hashem hides in the Megillah and in the world, and He waits for Jews to search for Him.
One who knows how to read the Megillah can read the world: the whole world is a greater Megillah full of hidden miracles for the sake of the Jewish people.
When Shushan Purim falls on Shabbos in Yerushalayim, the Megillah is not read, and the Rav says it is as if Hashem Himself reads it, and one must prepare to hear it.

title.en: Why Hashem's Name is hidden in the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav mentions this year's special Purim and that in Yerushalayim Purim lasts several days. He explains that on Purim holiness descends so low that Hashem's Name is not written in the Megillah, brings the Midrash that 'the King' there means Hashem, and says the Megillah's miracles are clothed in nature, which makes them greater.

title.en: The Name in order and reversed; the months

summary.en: The Rav sets out the rule: Hashem's Name in the initial letters of words, in order, is kindness; reversed or in the final letters it is judgment, since the yud gives and the heh receives. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that each month has its permutation of the Name, and shows how Nissan's pleasant spring and Tammuz's harsh heat match theirs.

title.en: The Name in the Megillah's verses

summary.en: The Rav shows Hashem's Name in verses of the Megillah: in order when Esther invites the king and Haman, reversed when Haman says 'all this is worth nothing to me', and in the final letters at the climax, when Haman's downfall was decided. He ties this to the Gemara's two blessings after the Megillah, for the downfall of the enemy and for the salvation of the Jews, and concludes that one must search the Megillah for where Hashem hides, as the Gemara finds Esther in 'I will surely hide My face'.

title.en: Reb Baruch'l's tears and today's hidden miracles

summary.en: The Rav tells how a child cried to Reb Baruch'l that he hid and nobody looked for him, and Reb Baruch'l wept that Hashem says the same. He then describes the daily miracles in Eretz Yisrael and in each Jew's life, which people do not notice, and the verses about Hashem's eyes resting on the land and on Yerushalayim.

title.en: The world as a greater Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Megillah's miracles happened within nature, a chain of events over nine years that could not happen by chance, and brings the Gemara that Memuchan was Haman, whose own advice led to his downfall. Whoever knows how to read the Megillah can read the news: the world is a greater Megillah, its leaders disguised players, and an honest Jew finds Hashem in everything, peering through the cracks.

title.en: The fifteenth of Adar, Yerushalayim and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav returns to this year's three-day Purim in Yerushalayim. He brings the Maharal that Esther asked for another day in Shushan so that somewhere Purim would fall on the fifteenth, when the moon is full, and links Yerushalayim to the moon. Since Shushan Purim falls on Shabbos and the Megillah is not read, he says Hashem Himself reads it, noting that the Mishnah says the Megillah 'is read', and urges preparing spiritual ears; he closes that Purim is a time for great salvations.

catalogTitle: The Candles Glow with the Light of משיח

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah candles reveal the hidden light of creation and the light of Moshiach, and shows how Moshiach ben Yosef was hidden in the story of Dina, Shechem and Osnas, a spark of holiness concealed in the lowest place.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the hidden light of the first day of creation, which Adam used for thirty-six hours and which Hashem hid in the Torah; it is found in the thirty-six tractates of Shas and in the thirty-six Chanukah candles. Bringing the Rokeach and the Bnei Yissaschar, he explains that the Chanukah light also reveals the light of Moshiach, which is why Chanukah has eight days. Moshiach comes in two stages, Moshiach ben Yosef, who fights Esav, and Moshiach ben David. He then tells, from the Targum Yonasan, how Osnas, the daughter of Dina and Shechem, came to marry Yosef, and shows that the seed of Moshiach ben Yosef was hidden in Shechem, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can. Like the Chanukah candle, which is lit below ten tefachim on the side of the Satan, Dina went down to draw holiness out of impurity. He ends with the wonders hidden in every word of Torah.

en: The hidden light of the first day, which Adam enjoyed for thirty-six hours, is hidden in the Torah and comes down to us in the thirty-six Chanukah candles.
The Chanukah light reveals the light of Moshiach, and Chanukah has eight days because eight belongs to Moshiach, above the seven of the natural world.
Moshiach comes in two parts: Moshiach ben Yosef, who wages the war against Esav, since Esav falls only to the children of Rachel, and then Moshiach ben David.
Hashem hides the roots of Moshiach in the lowest places, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can, so that the Satan should not look for it there.
The Chanukah candle is lit below ten tefachim and on the left side, the domain of the Satan, to find holiness there and draw it up, which is the way of Moshiach.
Dina was born to bring Moshiach ben Yosef into the world; she went out like the Chanukah candle into the domain of impurity to draw out holiness.

title.en: The hidden light and the thirty-six candles

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hidden light of the first day, which Adam used for thirty-six hours thanks to Shabbos, was hidden in the Torah, and that it comes down in the thirty-six tractates of Shas and the thirty-six Chanukah candles.

title.en: The light of Moshiach and the number eight

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rokeach on the thirty-six mentions of light in the Torah and the extra crowns on the first tes, and the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah light reveals the light of Moshiach. This is why Chanukah has eight days: eight, like the eight-stringed harp of the future, belongs to Moshiach.

title.en: Moshiach ben Yosef and the war against Esav

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshiach comes in two parts, Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David, and that Esav falls only to the children of Rachel. He relates the Chafetz Chaim's words about three wars, mentions the protection of seudah shlishis from the war of Gog and Magog, and says that both lights of Moshiach glow in the Chanukah candles, in Hallel and in Al Hanisim.

title.en: The story of Osnas, daughter of Dina

summary.en: From the Targum Yonasan and the Da'as Zekeinim, the Rav tells how Yaakov saved the child of Dina and Shechem, angels brought her to Egypt, Potiphar adopted her, and Yosef recognized her by his father's note on her necklace and married her.

title.en: A diamond hidden in a garbage can

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shechem carried a spark of Moshiach ben Yosef, hidden there as one hides a diamond from thieves in the garbage. He brings the Chasam Sofer that Dina went out to draw holiness out of the people of the land, and adds that she was sent out so that Moshiach ben Yosef, the adversary of Esav, should come out.

title.en: The candle in the domain of the Satan

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Gemara that the Shechinah never came down below ten tefachim with the Chanukah candle, which is lit below ten tefachim and on the left side, the side of the Satan. Chanukah goes down into his domain to find holiness and draw it up, and this, he says, is the meaning of Moshiach, who goes down to the lowest depths to bring up the Jews.

title.en: Yehuda, Yosef and Ovadia: treasures below

summary.en: The Rav shows that in the parshiyos of this week both Moshiach ben David, from Yehuda and Tamar, and Moshiach ben Yosef, from Yosef's descent, come out of low places. He brings Ovadia, a convert from Esav, who prophesies Esav's fall, like the axe handle taken from the forest, and announces that he will share wonders from the parshiyos of Kislev and Teves.

title.en: Why Dina: the exchange with Yosef

summary.en: The Rav asks why Dina of all people was to bring Moshiach ben Yosef, and answers from the Targum Yonasan and Rashi that Yosef was first conceived by Leah and Dina by Rachel, so Dina, originally Yosef, provided Yosef's match. He adds that the letters of Dina spelled out in full equal in gematria Moshiach ben Yosef.

title.en: Dina in the box, the hidden Chanukah light

summary.en: The Rav explains that Dina is the Chanukah light, born to go down into impurity and bring out Moshiach. Rashi's account of Yaakov hiding her in a box from Esav, because of Leah's debt to Esav, is no accident: she belongs concealed like the hidden light. He ends with a story of the Avnei Nezer showing wonders in every piece of Torah and with the passuk asking Hashem to uncover the eyes to see them.
